evidence_items.summary: Lithium-sulfur batteries cycle life is limited by dissolved Li$ y$S$ x^q$ polysulfides whose speciation remains disputed. We benchmark the complete matrix ($y$ = 0-2, $q$ = 0 to -2, $x$ = 1- 8) in the gas phase, tetraglyme and dimethyl sulfoxide: 248 M06-2X/SMD thermochemistries, 132 refined by single-point CCSD. The convex hull, S$ 8$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 6$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 4$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 3$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 2$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S, is identical in both solvents, and every exergonic long-chain comproportionation delivers Li$ 2$S$ 6$. QTAIM analysis of the CCSD densities separates covalent S--S from electrostatic Li--S bonding, transferably between solvents. Solvation makes S$ x^{2-}$ the dominant lithium-free charge state and places both legs of the shuttle on that branch. Infrared and Raman spectra of prepared solutions test the vibrational predictions and track the chain-length distribution through one band envelope. The open dataset of free energies, formation energies, QTAIM bond-critical-point and charge data, NBO data, vibrational modes, and optimized geometries provides a reference for benchmarking force-field, machine-learning, and continuum battery models.
evidence_items.title: Lithium polysulfide speciation benchmark: thermochemistry, bonding descriptors and vibrational data (companion dataset, v1.0.0)

evidence_items.summary: Research Data and Analysis Code for Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene This repository provides the archived molecular dynamics data, analysis scripts, processed datasets, and supplementary computational materials associated with the study entitled "Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene," submitted to Theoretical Chemistry Accounts. The study investigates the reconstruction and coarse-graining of electronic-state kinetic networks from a finite ensemble of 19 nonadiabatic surface-hopping trajectories of phosgene (COCl₂). The original simulations were performed using a TDDFT/TDA-PBE-based trajectory surface-hopping implementation within the Car–Parrinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) framework. The analysis reconstructs the complete 13-state singlet kinetic network from the observed electronic-state transitions and accumulated residence times. The original trajectory histories are subsequently mapped onto reduced kinetic representations, with effective rate constants re-estimated directly from the remapped trajectories. The repository consolidates the original computational archives and supporting analysis materials, including: Archived electronic-state histories and molecular-coordinate records from the phosgene surface-hopping simulations. Python scripts for kinetic-network reconstruction, population propagation, coarse-graining, and statistical validation. Computational workflows for grouped cross-validation, leave-one-trajectory-out analysis, bootstrap resampling, rare-channel sensitivity, and structural uncertainty assessment. Scripts and supporting materials for electronic-structure benchmarking, basis-set sensitivity analysis, and EOM-CCSD data extraction. Residence-time analysis and complementary kinetic and temporal diagnostics.
evidence_items.title: **Research Data and Analysis Code for Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene**  This repository provides the archived molecular dynamics data, analysis scripts, processed datasets, and supplementary computational materials associated with the study entitled "Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene," submitted to *Theoretical Chemistry Accounts*.  The study investigates the reconstruction and coarse-graining of electronic-state kinetic networks from a finite ensemble of 19 nonadiabatic surface-hopping trajectories of phosgene (COCl₂). The original simulations were performed using a TDDFT/TDA-PBE-based trajectory surface-hopping implementation within the Car–Parrinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) framework.  The analysis reconstructs the complete 13-state singlet kinetic network from the observed electronic-state transitions and accumulated residence times. The original trajectory histories are subsequently mapped onto reduced kinetic representations, with effective rate constants re-estimated directly from the remapped trajectories.  The repository consolidates the original computational archives and supporting analysis materials, including:  * Archived electronic-state histories and molecular-coordinate records from the phosgene surface-hopping simulations. * Python scripts for kinetic-network reconstruction, population propagation, coarse-graining, and statistical validation. * Computational workflows for grouped cross-validation, leave-one-trajectory-out analysis, bootstrap resampling, rare-channel sensitivity, and structural uncertainty assessment. * Scripts and supporting materials for electronic-structure benchmarking, basis-set sensitivity analysis, and EOM-CCSD data extraction. * Residence-time analysis and complementary kinetic and temporal diagnostics. * Structural and geometric analyses of the archived molecular trajectories, including periodic-image proximity assessments. * Selected processed datasets, numerical outputs, supplementary figures, source-package inventories, and SHA-256 checksums.  The original computational packages are preserved in their archived form, while the extracted analysis scripts and selected processed data are organized into a consolidated directory structure to facilitate inspection and reuse.  **Scope and limitations**  The deposited materials document the computational data and analysis procedures associated with the available 19-trajectory ensemble. The resulting kinetic parameters and reduced-state representations are conditional on the original electronic-structure model, trajectory sampling, and periodic simulation conditions.  The repository does not establish convergence of the original molecular dynamics ensemble, independent physical validation of the simulated S₁/S₀ transfer, or transferability of the inferred kinetic parameters to other molecular systems.  This consolidated workspace preserves the available source packages and supporting computational materials. Complete end-to-end reproduction of every result in the final revised manuscript has not yet been independently certified. Users should consult the included README, source-package documentation, and release-audit notes for information on individual workflows, input requirements, and known limitations.  The dataset is intended to support scientific transparency, methodological evaluation, and further research on kinetic reconstruction and coarse-graining of nonadiabatic molecular dynamics trajectories.

evidence_items.summary: © 2026 Elsevier B.V.Background: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)-only radiotherapy (RT) is increasingly adopted, but still lacks standardized commissioning procedures. This variability limits consistent clinical implementation: the Multicenter Evaluation of commercial Synthetic-Computed tomography ALgorithms (MESCAL) project aims to establish a benchmark dataset, provide commissioning guidelines, and define tolerance levels to support safe and reproducible MRI-only photon-beam RT adoption. Methods: Data from 32 patients (16 brain, 16 pelvis) were retrospectively collected from two centers. Four sCT solutions licensed for clinical use were evaluated: MRI Planner (Spectronic), SyngoAI (Siemens), MR Box (Therapanacea), and MRCAT (Philips). For each patient, multiple sCTs were generated and compared with the planning CT. Image quality was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and three additional indicators. Dose accuracy was evaluated by recalculating treatment plans on sCTs and performing dose–volume histogram (DVH) analysis. Position–verification accuracy was quantified by comparing CBCT–to–sCT versus CBCT–to–CT registrations. Plans meeting acceptability criteria (DVH differences < 2%, gamma-passing rate 95% at 2%/2 mm) were used to derive tolerance intervals. Results: Three to four sCTs were generated per case. Brain cases showed higher inter–software variability than pelvic cases, particularly in MAE within body (pelvis: 30–70 HU; brain: 40–130 HU). DVH differences remained within 3% (pelvis) and 4% (brain). Position–verification accuracy was higher in the brain (89% within 1 mm/1°) than in the pelvis (74%). Acceptability criteria were met by 37/43 pelvic and 30/39 brain plans: tolerance values were derived from these cases. Conclusion: MESCAL provides a commissioning framework, benchmark dataset, and tolerance levels to guide local sCT commissioning and promote standardized MRI-only photon-beam RT implementation.
evidence_items.title: Standardizing MRI-only radiotherapy commissioning: Benchmark dataset and acceptance levels from the MESCAL initiative

evidence_items.summary: Ultrathin multimode fiber (MMF) probes promise minimally invasive endoscopic access to sub-millimeter anatomy, but far-field imaging through a single small-core collection fiber yields severely speckle-dominated recordings dominated by multiplicative, signal-dependent interference that obscures fine structural details. While fully supervised physics-guided models achieve state-of-the-art despeckling fidelity with large-scale paired datasets, generating extensive clean ground truth (GT) references demands substantial experimental effort, limiting scalability in resource-constrained biomedical settings. Self-supervised approaches, conversely, struggle with the structured non-stationary patterns of coherent speckle due to their reliance on additive or pixel-independent noise models. We introduce a physics-informed, semi-supervised CycleGAN framework that overcomes these constraints by training primarily on abundant unpaired speckled patches augmented by only 1% clean references for identity regularization. Multiplicative speckle is converted to additive noise in the logarithmic domain; an attention-augmented UNet generator selectively preserves salient features; and optimal weighted convolution (OWC) modules embedded in outermost layers and discriminator input incorporate spatial density weighted prior that exploit the spatial correlation structure of coherent speckle patterns. Quantitative evaluations on paper and metal datasets demonstrate superior PSNR/SSIM over self-supervised baselines and standard CycleGAN, with reconstructions closely approaching fully supervised benchmarks without requiring paired speckled-clean data for training. This design offers a practical complement to paired training paradigms, enabling high-fidelity despeckling in scenarios where clean references are scarce-such as dynamic in vivo imaging, photon-limited deep-tissue probes, or clinical biopsies-thus advancing speckle-free ultrathin MMF endoscopy toward routine microanatomical interrogation.
evidence_items.title: Toward Practical Speckle-Free Imaging in Multimode Fiber Endoscopy via Semi-Supervised Cycle-Consistent Generative Networks With Optimal Weighted Convolution

evidence_items.summary: Purpose To evaluate the external transportability of source-derived probability calibration for chest radiograph deep learning classifiers under distribution shift and determine its dependence on sample size and disease prevalence. Materials and Methods This retrospective secondary computational analysis of public, de-identified radiographic datasets involved no participant contact or new data collection. Cohort sizes were prespecified by availability without prospective power calculation: 106,686 NIH ChestX-ray14 images (29,323 patients; 1992-2015) for development and internal testing, 20,000 CheXpert images (20,000 patients; October 2002-July 2017), and 14,998 VinBigData images (2018-2020) for external testing. ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and DeiT-Tiny classifiers for cardiomegaly and pleural effusion were trained across four patient fractions and three seeds (36 fits). Calibrators were fitted exclusively on NIH data. Twelve primary external Brier-score contrasts (temperature-scaled versus raw probabilities) were evaluated using paired cluster-bootstrapping with Holm adjustment. Results Temperature scaling reduced Brier scores in nine of 12 primary contrasts but worsened pleural effusion calibration on VinBigData across all architectures (Brier increases: ResNet-18, 0.001460 [95% CI: 0.001347, 0.001568]; DenseNet-121, 0.001193 [95% CI: 0.001109, 0.001274]; DeiT-Tiny, 0.000498 [95% CI: 0.000417, 0.000577]; all adjusted P=.006). Standardizing class weights to NIH prevalence reversed all CheXpert improvements. Although full versus 10% training improved external AUROC across all comparisons, DeiT-Tiny CheXpert pleural effusion Brier score worsened by 0.007039 despite a 0.032466 AUROC gain. At 80% selective image retention, calibrated ensembles retained only 12.3%-17.2% of VinBigData positive pleural effusion examinations.
evidence_items.title: Calibration, Uncertainty, and Data Efficiency of Deep Learning Chest Radiograph Classifiers Under Cross-Dataset Distribution Shift: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) systems transform natural-language questions into structured SPARQL queries to retrieve information from Knowledge Graphs (KGs). However, existing KGQA benchmarks are static, prone to obsolescence as KGs evolve, and increasingly unreliable for evaluating systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs) due to memorization effects (i.e. a model has reproduced the correct output from existing training data). This paper presents DynBench, a fully automated and robust framework for the dynamic generation of KGQA benchmark datasets. Unlike prior approaches, DynBench enables the automatic generation of an arbitrary number of new benchmark datasets while preserving the natural-language surface forms and structural complexity of the original SPARQL queries in comparison to the given original KGQA dataset. Using entity and property substitutions within the same KG, DynBench produces semantically consistent question-query pairs and automatically validates them without human intervention. We also introduce an automatic validation mechanism that ensures semantic and syntactic integrity through back-transformation and metric-based validation. Three dynamic benchmarks were generated from the well-known datasets QALD-9-plus, LC-QuAD 2.0, and RuBQ 2.0. After that, the new benchmarks were evaluated using both human experts and automated metrics to show DynBench’s dataset-agnostic capabilities. DynBench thus enables scalable, repeatable, and memorization-resistant dataset generation — providing a foundation for sustainable and fair evaluation of LLM-based KGQA systems. Therefore, the presented approach significantly contributes to solving the fundamental problem of automatically generating datasets with repeatable complexity that can also be versioned or regenerated as needed.
evidence_items.title: DynBench: Automated Scalable Robust Dynamic Generation of KGQA Benchmark Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Motivation: Peptide toxicity remains a major bottleneck in drug development, as small sequence variations can drastically alter cytotoxic profiles. Experimental assessment is costly and time-consuming, motivating computational predictors. Existing approaches often rely on single black-box architectures, limiting interpretability and obscuring the contribution of individual sequence features. Furthermore, benchmark datasets frequently define the negative class through annotation filters rather than direct experimental evidence, introducing structural label noise that can compromises training and evaluation. Results: We present NoiTox, a multi-model strategy for peptide toxicity prediction integrating three complementary architectures, evaluated as four model variants: NoiToxML (Bo/full), an Extremely Randomized Trees classifier with Boruta-selected or complete physicochemical, compositional, and atomic descriptors; NoiToxDP, a deep learning model leveraging ESM-2 protein language model embeddings; and NoiToxGP, a graph neural network that combines ESM-2 residue embeddings, a fully connected residue graph with attention, and the Boruta descriptors as global features. Averaged over five random seeds, the models approached the state-of-the-art predictor ToxiPep on CD-HIT-controlled test sets, and on an independent dataset the interpretable NoiToxML variants and a probability-averaging consensus of the four models exceeded it, showing that physicochemical descriptors are highly informative for toxicity prediction. Cross-referencing negative-labeled sequences against curated databases of hemolytic, cytotoxic, and neurotoxic peptides flagged a small set annotated as toxic elsewhere, consistent with label noise by omission.
evidence_items.title: NoiTox: A Machine Learning Strategy for Peptide Toxicity Prediction Reveals Label Noise in Benchmark Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Time-series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text-annotated time series pairs that are signal-grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re-deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross-channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one-off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time-series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person-days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time-series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health-outcome prediction. Caption-augmented training (OpenTSLM-Cap) outperforms a label-only baseline on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.
evidence_items.title: TimeCap: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Captioning Wearable Health Time-Series Data

evidence_items.summary: Graph Unlearning (GU) aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a Graph Neural Network without retraining anew. While most methods address removal of nodes and features, Edge Unlearning (EU), aiming at forgetting edges, has recently attracted dedicated attention as a standalone problem due to the hardness of completely removing the impact of an edge in the model. Despite this, no dedicated benchmark for EU exists besides isolated evaluations on feature-rich datasets such as Cora and Citeseer where GNNs exploit node features rather than graph structure. As such, we show two systematic limitations in existing evaluations: dedicated EU methods can be slower than retraining anew, and accuracy metrics are uninformative due to the negligible impact of edge removal. To address this gap, we introduce Lethe, the first comprehensive benchmark for Edge Unlearning, featuring 15 methods and 8 datasets. Our benchmark emphasizes large graphs, introduces evaluation tasks of varying difficulty, and proposes empirical measures based on link inference attacks rather than proxy accuracy metrics. We provide a comprehensive empirical analysis, demonstrate the shortcomings of current evaluations, and release Lethe as a reproducible, extensible benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Lethe: Link Inference Attacks For Evaluation of Edge Unlearning Methods

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate characterisation of the wound bed, the relative proportions of granulation, slough and necrotic tissue described by the red–yellow–black model, is central to monitoring healing and guiding debridement in chronic-wound care, yet in routine practice, it is judged visually and is poorly reproducible between clinicians. We investigated automatic, pixel-level segmentation of these three classes within the wound region of interest. A corpus of 404 photographs was curated from a public wound image collection and densely annotated by wound care clinicians with a purpose-built, cluster-assisted labelling tool. Five deep learning architectures spanning convolutional, transformer, hybrid and ensemble families were trained on one frozen data split under a largely shared pipeline, with limited, fully documented architecture-specific tuning, and scored on a shared 62-image test set. The models fell within a narrow mean intersection-over-union band (0.748–0.818). The strongest single model, a purely convolutional network, was statistically indistinguishable from the best ensemble, and simply averaging already-trained convolutional and transformer models matched that ensemble at no additional training cost. Slough remained consistently the hardest tissue. Translated into clinical units, per-wound tissue percentages were recovered with small mean bias (within ± 5 percentage points) but wide single-image limits of agreement (about ± 25–50 percentage points), so the measurement suits aggregate and longitudinal assessment rather than single-image reading. Within this dataset, split and training protocol, the choice among the strong hierarchical architectures was not decisive: a single strong model is the pragmatic option for clinical deployment, with an ensemble reserved for maximal accuracy and class balance.
evidence_items.title: Automated Segmentation of Wound Bed Tissue from Clinical Photographs: A Benchmark of Five Deep Learning Architectures Under a Shared Protocol

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.
evidence_items.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Clinical temporal relation extraction (CTRE) is essential for reconstructing patient timelines from unstructured electronic health records (EHRs). However, the linguistic complexity of clinical notes and the high cost of expert annotation impede the development of large-scale training corpora. While large language models (LLMs) have transformed general natural language processing, their application to CTRE remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to determine the optimal adaptation strategy for CTRE by conducting a controlled comparative benchmarking of LLM architectures and fine-tuning methodologies in both data-rich and limited-data regimes. Methods We evaluated 4 LLMs representing 2 distinct architectures—transformer encoders (GatorTron [University of Florida and NVIDIA]) and transformer decoders (LLaMA 3.1-8B [Meta AI] and MeLLaMA-13B [Yale University and University of Florida]). We compared four adaptation strategies: (1) standard fine-tuning, (2) hard-prompting, (3) soft-prompting, and (4) low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Experiments were conducted on the 2012 i2b2 CTRE benchmark in both full-supervision and 1-shot scenarios. Results Recent LLMs combined with appropriate adaptation strategies achieved strong performance for CTRE on the 2012 i2b2 benchmark. In the data-rich setting, the best-performing configuration was LLaMA3.1-8B with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) applied to the query and value projection layers, achieving a micro- F 1 score of 89.15% (0.30). Comparative analyses showed that QLoRA applied only to the query and value projection layers achieved performance comparable to QLoRA applied to all linear layers, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Hard-prompting showed particular effectiveness in the 1-shot scenario compared with standard fine-tuning for GatorTron-Base. Overall, Decoder-based models generally outperformed encoder-based models under QLoRA-based adaptation.
evidence_items.title: Optimizing Clinical Temporal Relation Extraction With Large Language Models: Comparative Analysis

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are critical candidates for addressing the global antibiotic resistance crisis. AI‐driven quantitative models capable of directly predicting peptide antimicrobial activity, specifically minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), are gaining scientific prominence by providing precise guidance for the rational design of AMPs. To assess their real‐world, out‐of‐the‐box performance, we conducted a retrospective benchmark of 10 publicly released quantitative AMP prediction tools spanning classical machine learning and contemporary deep learning approaches. Using an external dataset and reconstructed native datasets, we evaluated absolute MIC regression, retrospective reproducibility, directional prediction patterns, ranking capability, and virtual‐screening enrichment. Most released tools exhibited poor absolute MIC regression and limited transferability to the external benchmark, while selected tools retained useful relative‐ranking and enrichment capabilities. Retrospective evaluation further revealed marked differences in implementation‐level reproducibility among the released tools. Error‐stratified analyses identified systematic associations between prediction errors and peptide residue composition, together with a general compression of the predicted activity range. Collectively, these findings characterize the practical performance boundaries of currently accessible quantitative AMP prediction tools and support their use primarily as early‐stage screening filters rather than precise substitutes for experimental MIC measurements.
evidence_items.title: A Retrospective Benchmark of Quantitative Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction Tools

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate representations of porous microstructures are essential for studying transport and effective properties in geomaterials such as clay, carbonate, and sandstone. Deep generative models provide a means of producing additional statistically representative microstructures, but different model families can differ substantially in their ability to reproduce morphology, population variability, and transport-relevant connectivity. In this work, we present a comparative benchmark of three generative-model families for porous microstructure synthesis: a Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP), denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), and flow matching models. The benchmark considers six microstructure datasets in two dimensionally consistent settings: two-dimensional models trained on 2D images and supervised three-dimensional models trained on 3D volumes. The comparison therefore addresses 2D-to-2D and 3D-to-3D synthesis rather than dimensional expansion from 2D to 3D. Model performance is assessed using visual comparison, phase statistics, and microstructure-relevant structural descriptors, with effective diffusivity additionally evaluated for the three-dimensional benchmark. Across the considered datasets, all three model families reproduce important aspects of the reference microstructures, although their relative performance depends on the quantity being assessed. Flow matching is comparatively consistent across the reported structural measures and, in three dimensions, reproduces the reference porosity--diffusivity relation most consistently. It also requires substantially fewer sequential sampling evaluations than the 1,000-step DDPM configuration considered here, while WGAN-GP retains the advantage of single-pass generation.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Benchmark of GAN, DDPM, and Flow Matching for 2D and 3D Porous Microstructures Synthesis.

evidence_items.summary: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.
evidence_items.title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.
evidence_items.title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?

evidence_items.summary: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
evidence_items.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation

evidence_items.summary: Medical calculators translate raw patient observations into clinically actionable values and scores. However, applying these calculators directly to free-form patient notes requires precise variable extraction combined with the exact execution of complex formulas, scoring rules, and output conventions. Relying solely on direct large language model (LLM) prompting is unreliable in this context, as rule recall, parameter extraction, arithmetic reasoning, and formatting become entangled within a single generative step. To address these limitations, we propose a tool-augmented LLM framework for reliable medical calculation from patient notes. The framework retrieves and structures calculator specifications, generates reusable executable tools, and uses a constrained extractor to map each patient note to calculator-ready inputs. The tools then perform deterministic calculation, separating clinical language understanding from rule execution and arithmetic. Evaluated on the MedCalc-Bench dataset, our method achieves 86.73% final-answer accuracy, outperforming the one-shot prompting and supervised fine tuning-only baselines by 24.0 and 17.27 percentage points. Ablation and error analyses show that these performance gains are primarily driven by rule-grounded tool synthesis and schema-constrained extraction, whereas remaining failures are concentrated in clinical-semantic extraction and benchmark-specific output contracts. By grounding calculator logic in executable tools, the proposed approach alleviates arithmetic hallucinations and improves the computational reliability of the final clinical outputs.
evidence_items.title: Tool-Augmented Large Language Models for Reliable Medical Calculation from Patient Notes

evidence_items.summary: Decision trees can make vision-language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root-to-leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non-backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce \textbf{MYOPIA}, a benchmark comprising four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset--model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero-shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree-encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label--image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model-dependent loss. A node-level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding differences are less stable. \textbf{MYOPIA} therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.
evidence_items.title: MYOPIA: Understanding the Limits of Tree-Based Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
evidence_items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
evidence_items.title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents'tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use

evidence_items.summary: Generative models often produce perceptually plausible outputs that violate hard domain rules. In architectural layout generation, balancing geometric intuition with regulatory compliance remains a persistent challenge, as current frameworks routinely fail to conform to local building laws. This paper proposes LayoutGen, a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework coupling probabilistic generation with deterministic verification in an evaluation-guided refinement loop. LayoutGen employs a four-phase retrieval-driven pipeline (spatial reasoning, coordinate mapping, vector rendering, and iterative refinement) powered by a dual retrieval engine leveraging architectural precedents and legislative laws. An Evaluation Engine scores the generated 2D Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) layouts and returns a graded, itemised report. Every scored quantity is computed by deterministic geometric checks over the generated coordinates against a structured rule repository; the Large Language Model (LLM) is confined to spatial planning, coordinate proposal, and the natural language feedback that drives refinement, together with an advisory Vaastu commentary that does not enter the grade. Evaluated on single-storey residential configurations drawn from the RPLAN and MSD datasets, spanning studio to 3BHK typologies and represented as axisaligned rectangular rooms, the full pipeline reduces detected violations from 3.7 to 0.3 per plan across n=200 runs, a 92% reduction relative to an unretrieved, unrefined single-shot baseline using the same backbone model. Violations are counted across the three error categories the Evaluation Engine checks: topological, geometric, and the encoded dimensional provisions of minimum room area, minimum room width and critical width. The regulatory component of that count covers only provisions decidable from single-floor room geometry; setbacks, floor area ratio, egress, staircase geometry, parking and ventilation are present in the repositories but checked outside the generation loop. Component ablation isolates the contribution of each pipeline stage, and the same architecture runs unchanged across three Indian municipal rule repositories (BBMP, CMDA, GHMC) through structured rule replacement alone, without retraining or prompt redesign. These three regimes express their dimensional provisions in a common form, so this establishes portability within that family rather than generality across regulatory systems. The framework also integrates Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time design streaming.
evidence_items.title: An evaluation guided multiagent framework for generating floor plans that comply with municipal building regulations

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishonesty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model's hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data.
evidence_items.title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty

evidence_items.summary: We use quantum machine learning techniques to develop a content-based media recommender system and evaluate its performance on TV programmes using textual descriptions from one week of BBC iPlayer data. Grounded in the Quantum Natural Language Processing framework (QNLP), programme synopses are mapped to variational quantum circuits using their semantic structure. The parameters of these circuits are trained via a supervised pairwise similarity learning task. We benchmark the quantum recommender against a classical BiLSTM baseline trained on the same dataset and objective. While both models achieve comparable performance on the similarity learning task, the quantum model requires significantly fewer parameters (47k vs. 17.8M). When the BiLSTM is constrained to a matching parameter budget, its performance degrades substantially (by 3.63 percentage points in Mean Average Precision (MAP)), indicating that the structured quantum representation provides a highly parameter-efficient alternative in this setting. We demonstrate the feasibility of executing the trained models on quantum hardware by deploying the circuits on Quantinuum's System Model H2 (and accompanying emulator) using a SWAP-test-based protocol. The results confirm that the similarity signal is preserved under realistic, noisy conditions. Taken together, these findings highlight the potential of variational quantum circuits for recommendation tasks and represent a practical step toward their real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: A Quantum Machine Learning Approach to Content-Based Media Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
evidence_items.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe

evidence_items.summary: Diagnosing brain tumors from MRI scans is technically challenging but necessary. Early and correct characterization provides direct indications for subsequent treatment of and survival of the patient. While deep learning models show accuracy, most of them focus on just one classification task lacking practical tools for clinical use. We introduce Modified DenseNet121 (Dual-Task framework built on a modified DenseNet121 with a custom regularization stack. This is important to detect abnormalities (Normal vs. Abnormal) and identify three tumor types (Glioma, Meningioma, and Pituitary) in a single architecture. The model incorporates Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) for qualitative spatial interpretability, and the model is set up within a PyQt5 desktop research prototype illustrating real-time dual prediction with typical inference latency of 80–130 ms (mean: 185.80 ± 402.83 ms; median: 127.99 ms; 95th percentile: 134.65 ms), probability visualization, Grad-CAM heatmap overlay, and feedback recording from the physician. Elaborate benchmarking experiments were performed against six competing CNN architectures DenseNet121 (baseline), ConvNeXtSmall, ConvNeXtTiny, EfficientNetB0, NASNetMobile and Xception over two large, publicly available MRI datasets: dataset 1, Kaggle, holding 7023 images; and dataset 2, Mendeley, having 12,064 images. Modified DenseNet121 achieved 99.85% binary accuracy and 99.00% multiclass accuracy on dataset 1, and 99.62% binary accuracy and 99.00% multiclass accuracy on dataset 2, achieving competitive performance with all benchmark architectures across both datasets. The zero-shot evaluation on an additional publicly available external MRI dataset achieved 99.75% binary accuracy and 99.20% multiclass accuracy, demonstrating transfer performance under an external evaluation setting. However, because dedicated image-level overlap analysis was not performed, these results are interpreted as evidence of external transfer performance rather than definitive evidence of complete dataset independence. The experimental results demonstrate high predictive performance across two large publicly available datasets and verify the technical feasibility of Modified DenseNet121 as a robust research prototype. This study offers reproducible, interpretable, and research prototype foundation for future clinical translation of neuro-oncological computer-aided diagnosis systems.
evidence_items.title: A modified dual-task DenseNet121 with Grad-CAM interpretability for brain tumor classification from MRI

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to address the information security governance issues associated with the use of AI in HRM by developing the artificial intelligence–human resource management (AI-HRM) cybersecurity architecture (AHCA), a novel domain-specific architecture.
 
 
 
 The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles, and 72 peer-reviewed papers were obtained from journals indexed in Scopus and IEEE Xplore, or from CORE-ranked journals, for the years 2020–2025, with citation chaining in Google Scholar. Three research questions guided the synthesis, covering threat conceptualisation, security implications and governance. This study then created the AHCA following an iterative design science process, using each component directly from literature reviews, and constructed a structured rubric with explicit anchoring examples to enable replication of the comparative evaluation.
 
 
 
 The review identified six categories of AI-HRM security threats: data breaches (T1), exploitation of algorithmic bias (T2), insider threat amplification (T3), model poisoning attacks (T4), regulatory non-compliance (T5) and governance and audit failures (T6). There is a wide disparity in the attention these subjects receive in the literature: algorithmic bias (43.1 %) and governance and audit failure (51.4 %) together account for 94.4 % of the corpus whose primary focus could be coded, while data breaches (1.4 %), insider threat (1.4 %) and regulatory non-compliance (2.8 %) sit at the margins, and no study takes model poisoning as its primary focus. In addition, most governance-oriented research identifies accountability gaps but stops short of architectural solutions. The AHCA is designed to address this structural deficit, pairing four-layer architecture with a 14-indicator security performance indicator (SPI) framework.
 
 
 
 The corpus is limited to English-language publications from 2020 to 2025 that appear in journals in the AHCA’s Q1 or Q2 tiers, and the AHCA itself is a design artefact that will be tested in practice through Delphi panels of experts and longitudinal case studies. The technical security literature emerged when searching IEEE Xplore and Scopus; a complementary search of the ACM Digital Library is planned as a future extension.
 
 
 
 The AHCA and its SPI framework offer HR practitioners and policymakers an AI-HRM-specific blueprint for general data protection regulation (GDPR) compliant, high-risk employment systems in accordance with the provisions of the European Union AI Act.
 
 
 
 The AHCA incorporates GDPR and EU AI Act compliance-by-design principles into a single HRM-specific security architecture that is currently in the early phases of development. It is the only benchmark that addresses the HRM-specific and EU AI Act dimensions, which are not addressed by sector-agnostic comparators, and it performs well in the generic HRM security dimensions on a replicable nine-dimension rubric, benchmarked against NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, ISO 27001 and NIST CSF.
evidence_items.title: Securing artificial intelligence in human resource management: a systematic review and the AI-HRM cybersecurity architecture (AHCA)

evidence_items.summary: With the increasing complexity of smart home environments, trigger-action-program (TAP) conflicts have emerged as critical issues, occurring when multiple automation apps compete for control over shared devices or interact in unintended ways. While existing approaches detect and resolve such conflicts using predefined rules or expert knowledge, they fail to account for the significant variability in individual pReferences for conflict resolution and significantly degrade the automation-system utility. To address this gap, we propose a preference-aligned conflict resolution (PaCR), a novel agentic framework that resolves conflicts while aligning with users’ personalized preferences for automation behavior. PaCR employs a two-step conflict resolution process: first, it interactively gathers contextual information from smart home configurations to generate conflict resolution agents (CRAs) with user profiles that accurately depict user preferences and characteristics; then, the agents, acting as users, utilize the semantic reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to assist in generating personalized conflict detection and resolution strategies. Due to the agentic conflict-resolving feature, we evaluate the effectiveness of PaCR with existing datasets at scale. PaCR demonstrates strong capabilities in addressing conflicts based on users’ needs and significantly improves conflict resolution efficacy and interpretability, offering a user-centric approach to managing smart-home automation conflicts.
evidence_items.title: PaCR: An Agentic Preference-Aligned TAP Conflict Handling

evidence_items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
evidence_items.title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following

evidence_items.summary: Well stimulation remains essential for improving reservoir productivity, but conventional workflows are constrained by geological heterogeneity, limited data, and dependence on empirical correlations. This systematic and comparative review examines artificial-intelligence applications in hydraulic fracturing, acidizing, sand control, and ultrasonic stimulation, focusing on 2020–2025 while selectively considering earlier foundational studies. The quantitative synthesis of 23 key application studies identified 11 studies on acidizing and acid fracturing (47.8%), 8 on hydraulic fracturing (34.8%), 3 on sand control (13.0%), and 1 on ultrasonic stimulation (4.3%). Neural-network architectures were reported in 16 studies (69.6%), while tree-based learners or ensembles appeared in 13 studies (56.5%); these categories overlap because several studies compared multiple algorithms. Among studies reporting numerical performance, R2 values for acidizing-related regression tasks ranged from 0.82 to 0.96, while reported classification accuracies for selected acidizing and sand-control applications ranged from 87.5% to above 90%. These values were not statistically pooled because the studies used different prediction targets, data scales, validation procedures, and performance definitions. Tree-based ensembles and neural networks currently dominate fracture-design and acidizing applications, whereas reinforcement learning, hybrid optimization, and physics-informed approaches remain less frequently investigated. Field-scale and cross-field validation are limited, particularly for sand control and ultrasonic stimulation, for which the available evidence is predominantly laboratory- or simulation-based. The principal barriers to operational deployment are proprietary and small datasets, inconsistent validation, limited interpretability, and uncertain model transferability. Future research should prioritize benchmark datasets, standardized reporting, external field validation, explainable and physics-constrained models, and carefully evaluated closed-loop stimulation systems. Provides an integrated cross-method review of AI applications in hydraulic fracturing, acidizing, sand control, and ultrasonic stimulation, with emphasis on model selection, field readiness, and closed-loop decision support. Proposes a taxonomy of AI models (supervised, unsupervised, deep learning, hybrid/physics-informed) with comparative analysis of strengths, limitations, and use cases. Introduces updated literature tables and figures that map AI adoption trends, stimulation-specific applications, and research gaps. Identifies key challenges including data scarcity, model interpretability, limited field deployment, and underrepresentation of sand control and ultrasonic stimulation. Outlines future directions and strategic recommendations for industry adoption, emphasizing explainable AI, benchmark datasets, real-time control, and ESG-aligned workflows. Provides an integrated cross-method review of AI applications in hydraulic fracturing, acidizing, sand control, and ultrasonic stimulation, with emphasis on model selection, field readiness, and closed-loop decision support. Proposes a taxonomy of AI models (supervised, unsupervised, deep learning, hybrid/physics-informed) with comparative analysis of strengths, limitations, and use cases. Introduces updated literature tables and figures that map AI adoption trends, stimulation-specific applications, and research gaps. Identifies key challenges including data scarcity, model interpretability, limited field deployment, and underrepresentation of sand control and ultrasonic stimulation. Outlines future directions and strategic recommendations for industry adoption, emphasizing explainable AI, benchmark datasets, real-time control, and ESG-aligned workflows.
evidence_items.title: A systematic and critical review of artificial intelligence applications for enhancing well stimulation operations and sustainable reservoir management

evidence_items.summary: Background: NOHARM scores a language model's management plan for a real primary-care-to-specialist consultation against specialists' ratings of the actions the case calls for. Most severe errors are omissions. The public leaderboard scores models on the bare case, with no instruction. Objective: To measure how much a structured instruction changes these scores, which part of the instruction matters, and whether the extra content is safe. Methods: On the 30 public cases (330 items), twelve models answered the bare case and five also answered with an instruction. An AI evaluator applied the benchmark's own scoring. On two models we tested the instruction's parts separately, against a plain request for 25 recommendations. Model raters and a physician reviewed the added actions the rubric does not cover. Intervals come from resampling whole cases. Results: The instruction raised severity-weighted F1 by 0.14 on average [0.09, 0.20], most for the tersest models: GPT-5.6 terra rose from 0.678 to 0.853 and Grok 4.7 from 0.354 to 0.633. The spread between models halved (standard deviation 0.17 to 0.09). Taken apart on Sonnet 5.5 and terra, the plan format alone matched the full instruction, while the request for 25 recommendations produced as many actions but scored lower (-0.040 [-0.069, -0.015] for Sonnet 5.5, -0.084 [-0.148, -0.029] for terra). Most recovered actions were follow-up and counselling. Instructed Sonnet proposed +0.13 [+0.05, +0.23] more specialist-rated harmful options per item, mostly mild or moderate; a physician reading them in context judged none harmful, and judged none of the 72 unlisted actions that a model rater had flagged as harmful to be inappropriate. One instructed call scored level with a four-call system (+0.004 [-0.035, +0.041]).
evidence_items.title: Asking for the Whole Plan: Prompt Design Moves Language Models’ Scores on a Clinical-Safety Benchmark More Than Model Choice: An Exploratory Study on the NOHARM v2 Public Cases

evidence_items.summary: The Cox proportional hazards (CPH) model and the exponential Cox model are foundational tools in survival analysis, yet they impose structural assumptions; proportional hazards and constant baseline hazard, respectively that frequently fail in practice. This paper proposes and evaluates pooled logistic regression (PLR) applied to survival-piled (stacked) data as an alternative discrete-time survival estimator. Right-censored survival data are restructured into a long-format person-time binary classification dataset, and three models are compared: the exponential Cox model, the classical semi-parametric CPH model, and PLR. Monte Carlo simulations with 1,000 replications at each of six sample sizes (n = 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250) are conducted to assess stability, discrimination, and goodness-of-fit. Performance is measured by Harrell's concordance index (C-index) and the Akaike information criterion (AIC). Simulation results show that PLR maintains consistently high and stable C-index values (0.742–0.784) across all sample sizes, whereas the CPH model exhibits high variability (0.575–0.884) and the exponential Cox model underperforms throughout (0.532–0.671). AIC comparisons further demonstrate PLR's competitive goodness-of-fit at moderate and large sample sizes. Real-data validation using the NCCTG lung cancer dataset corroborates these findings. PLR's theoretical connection to the Cox partial likelihood is established formally, and its compatibility with machine-learning classification pipelines is discussed. The findings support PLR as a robust, flexible, and interpretable alternative for discrete-time survival analysis.
evidence_items.title: Efficiency of the Pooled Logistic Regression Approach as an Alternative to the Cox Proportional Hazard Model

evidence_items.summary: This dataset preserves the accepted R6.5.4.5 controlled paired local HTTP/3 experiment for NGI541. The experiment compares two server-side cryptographic execution paths under the same application protocol, workload objects, network path, and measurement rules. Baseline configuration.NGINX QUIC/HTTP/3 with the standard OpenSSL-based server-side cryptographic path. In the internal experiment labeling, this variant is named stock. Candidate configuration.The same NGINX QUIC/HTTP/3 server, configured so that the supported QUIC AES-GCM packet-protection operations and AES-based QUIC header-protection operations are executed through NGI541. In the internal experiment labeling, this variant is named ngi541-direct. TLS 1.3 handshake processing, certificate validation, and the surrounding QUIC/HTTP/3 protocol logic remain under NGINX/OpenSSL in both variants. The comparison is therefore scoped to a controlled substitution in the server-side cryptographic execution path rather than to a full protocol-stack replacement. The archived material contains the accepted publication bundle, frozen execution provenance, paired result summary, methods, per-condition measurements, integrity information, and supporting visualizations. The scientific workload inputs are deterministic object profiles representing three data-movement styles: CLAS12 event-stream style objects LCLS detector-frame style objects HACC multifile-dataset style objects These are deterministic benchmark object models for controlled experimentation and are not original collaboration datasets.
evidence_items.title: NGI541: Controlled Paired HTTP/3 Cryptographic Execution Benchmark Dataset (R6.5.4.5)

evidence_items.summary: This research record provides reproducibility artifacts supporting a study of offline fault classification and causal online alarm reliability in multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles. The package contains C and Python implementations, logistic regression and Random Forest comparison results, derived evaluation tables, integrity checksums, and experimental timing measurements obtained on a physical Raspberry Pi 4. The evaluation uses 18 UAV-FD flight recordings comprising six nominal and twelve damaged-propeller flights. Three decision strategies are examined: whole-file aggregation, immediate single-window alarms, and causally filtered alarm decisions. Embedded validation includes a one-hour prerecorded-data replay involving 360,000 samples and eight selected frequency-controlled experiments, with four runs at 600 MHz and four at 1500 MHz. Across these experiments, no 10-ms deadline violations were observed under the tested conditions. These experiments use prerecorded sensor data rather than live ArduPilot acquisition. They do not establish deterministic worst-case execution-time guarantees or validate real radio-frequency communication performance. The original UAV-FD flight recordings are not redistributed in this repository. They are available from the original dataset published by Baldini et al. (2023), DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7648996 . The repository is intended to support reproducibility, independent verification, and further research in embedded fault diagnosis, multirotor systems, and reliable UAV monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Reproducibility Artifacts for UAV-FD Multirotor Fault Alarms: Cross-Detector Evaluation and Raspberry Pi 4 Frequency-Controlled Replay

evidence_items.summary: Semantic retrieval systems, which match a user query to relevant content by comparing vector embeddings rather than exact keywords, have become the backbone of modern search, question answering, and conversational assistant applications. Their central strength, finding content that is conceptually related even when the wording differs, is also the source of a persistent weakness. Embeddings that sit close together in vector space are not always close together in intent, and a retrieval system that cannot tell the difference will confidently return a confidently wrong result. This article examines intent confusion as a distinct failure mode in semantic retrieval and presents selective index suppression as a targeted strategy for reducing it without sacrificing the recall benefits that make semantic retrieval valuable in the first place. Selective index suppression withholds specific index entries, or entire regions of embedding space, from consideration at query time when the evidence suggests those entries are more likely to confuse intent than to serve it. This article presents the conceptual basis for intent confusion in embedding space, a taxonomy of suppression strategies, the precision and recall tradeoffs these strategies introduce, the index architecture required to support them, and an evaluation methodology for measuring their effect. The approach draws on established practice in information retrieval, dense passage retrieval research, and vector search infrastructure to ground its recommendations in observed research and engineering practice [1][4][5]. The article is organized into thirteen sections, moving from the intent confusion problem and embedding space visualization, through suppression strategy taxonomy, precision and recall tradeoffs, index architecture, evaluation methodology, governance, benchmarking data, and a quantitative analysis of the operational and financial case for investment.
evidence_items.title: REDUCING INTENT CONFUSION: SELECTIVE INDEX SUPPRESSION STRATEGIES FOR HIGH-PRECISION SEMANTIC RETRIEVAL

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM--MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Eight single-model pipelines generated independent role-specific opinions and interactive-consilium reports under free-form and structured clinical-reasoning conditions. A physician-calibrated LLM Judge evaluated 3,040 final reports and the corresponding structured primary-role outputs. Model identity separated report quality more strongly than response format. Structured final reports had higher overall mean scores in seven of eight model pipelines, with their clearest advantage in management (2.740 vs. 2.436). Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation.
evidence_items.title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions

evidence_items.summary: Fine jewelry retailers must reconcile uncertain demand, high-value inventory, complex material histories, and expectations of responsible sourcing. This article develops a responsible artificial intelligence framework that connects demand forecasting, provenance evidence, and governance within retail planning. A conceptual framework-development approach informed by design-science research combines a targeted literature update through October 9, 2026, with descriptive analysis of published market statistics and an external retail forecasting benchmark. The analysis distinguishes original design propositions from empirical findings reported by other researchers; no retailer-level experiment or environmental impact assessment was conducted. Three sourced bar charts illustrate changing gold jewelry consumption and the methodological relevance of inventory-based model evaluation. The resulting architecture integrates data inputs, predictive analytics, provenance and traceability, ethical governance, and human-reviewed decisions with feedback. Five design principles and five testable propositions specify how forecasts can inform assortment, replenishment, allocation, and sourcing while preserving evidence quality and accountability. The framework shifts evaluation from forecast accuracy alone toward decision quality under explicit operational and provenance constraints. It also separates inventory efficiency, sourcing documentation, and environmental outcomes, preventing improvements in one category from being misrepresented as proof of another. Managerial implications include staged implementation, evidence-qualified sourcing rules, meaningful review authority, and documented overrides. Future validation should compare complete decision policies, preserve temporal information boundaries, measure calibrated reliance, and assess environmental consequences independently.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Forecast Accuracy: A Responsible AI Framework for Provenance-Aware Fine Jewelry Retail Planning

evidence_items.summary: ABMForge is an open-source Python framework for agent-based modelling and simulation experiments, designed to support structured experiment specification, reproducible execution, linked scientific observations, validated result archives, and conservative reuse of previously completed simulations. This repository preserves the evaluated research version ABMForge 0.3.0a2.dev4 and the associated experimental evidence supporting the manuscript “ABMForge for Agent-Based Simulation Experiments with Validated Result Archives.” Software and Research Contributions ABMForge integrates agent-based model construction, scenario configuration, parameterized experiments, structured data recording, and archive management within a unified Python workflow. A central feature is its archive-backed recovery mechanism, which validates persisted evidence and execution identities before determining whether a completed simulation can be reused. The accompanying research workflow explicitly associates retained and newly generated observations with revised experimental selections while preserving historical baselines. Experimental Evaluation The software was evaluated against Mesa 3.5.1 using matched agent-based simulation workflows and observed workplace contact networks from SocioPatterns. The main evaluation included: 92 participants and 9,827 observed contact records. Ten observed day offsets and multiple network and protection configurations. Four execution workflows: ABMForge fresh execution, ABMForge archive reuse, Mesa fresh execution, and Mesa with an independently implemented caching layer. 4,216 native simulation executions representing 680 distinct logical requests. Exact agreement in selected initial states, agent trajectories, and scientific metrics across all four workflows. A 49.4% reduction in required simulation executions for both reuse-enabled workflows under the prescribed revision protocol. Independent verification of 11,636,160 agent state transitions.
evidence_items.title: ABMForge 0.3.0a2.dev4: Evaluated Source and Reproducibility Artifact

evidence_items.summary: Real-Time Simulator for Fractional-Order Thermal Control is an open-source web-based educational and research platform for the simulation of thermoelectric cooling systems. The software implements a calibrated three-node thermal digital twin identified from experimental data obtained from a real Peltier module. A fractional-order PID (FOPID) controller based on the Grünwald–Letnikov discrete approximation enables real-time tuning of Kp, Ki, Kd, λ, and μ parameters. The platform consists of a Python WebSocket server and a browser-based graphical interface requiring no installation. Users can modify controller parameters, ambient conditions, relative humidity, operating modes, and experiment duration while observing the closed-loop thermal response in real time. The simulator provides performance metrics including RMSE, MAE, undershoot, settling time, rise time, steady-state error, and energy consumption. Results can be exported as CSV datasets and PNG reports. The software was developed for engineering education, control-system training, digital twin research, and reproducible experimentation in thermal control applications. v2.1: corrected FOPID implementation (Grünwald-Letnikov weights, integral accumulator, anti-windup), 0.1 s sampling period.

evidence_items.summary: This qualitative document analysis synthesized published research and official documents concerning reading comprehension, content-area literacy, storytelling, and contextualized reading for Key Stage 2 AralingPanlipunan (AP). Seventeen publicly accessible documents dated 2021–2026 were purposively selected and examined using a structured coding matrix and reflexive thematic analysis. Six themes were developed: persistent reading-comprehension difficulties alongside reported improvements in Philippine assessments; the contribution of language and background knowledge; benefits and limits of integrated literacy and content instruction; associations between story-based approaches and language or literacy outcomes; the importance of medium and multimedia design; and inconsistent evidence concerning motivation as a pathway to comprehension. None of the documents in the selected corpus directly evaluated the combined use of interactive storytelling and contextualized passages in Key Stage 2 AP. A six-component, literature-derived instructional framework was therefore proposed, encompassing knowledge activation, interactive story delivery, contextualized passage reading, multimedia design, engagement support, and delivery-medium decisions. The framework was not empirically tested or validated. The synthesis offers a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently evaluating AP instructional materials, rather than evidence that the proposed approach improves learner outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Storytelling and Contextualized Reading Passages for Key Stage 2 Araling Panlipunan: A Qualitative Document Analysis
