evidence_items.summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
evidence_items.title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

evidence_items.summary: Misinformation is common in online media, including in health-related content. Such misinformation constitutes a significant risk to the medical-demographic security of the population. Many people actively seek medical information online without the ability to verify its trustworthiness. This paper proposes a modular system for automated detection of misinformation in medical content based on retrieval-augmented verification. In the pipeline, input articles are summarized and decomposed into atomic claims. Each claim is then vectorized using dense embeddings (BGE-Large-en-v1.5) and matched against a self-constructed knowledge base via cosine similarity to retrieve evidence. Retrieved evidence is verified using large language model (LLM)- based natural language inference (NLI) and aggregated into article-level predictions through a scoring function. The LLM used in the system is the open-source LLaMA-3.1 model with eight billion parameters. Together with a self-contained knowledge base, this represents a deliberately constrained environment. Such a setup isolates the contribution of the presented architecture from its dependency on external knowledge sources and LLMs with large parameter counts. The system achieved 98.4% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.978 at 79.0% coverage on the evaluated datasets (DETERRENT and CONSTRAINT). This demonstrates that, even under resource constraints, the correct pipeline architecture enables high-precision misinformation detection on medical content. It also represents a clear improvement over the ablation experiment, which used the same model without the proposed pipeline and achieved an F1 of only 0.773.
evidence_items.title: Detecting Health Misinformation Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering, summarisation, coding, and research support, yet choosing a suitable model remains difficult because models differ in performance, context capacity, cost, privacy, and deployment options. This paper presents a document-based comparative analysis of five LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, and Mistral Large 2. Using published technical reports, official documentation, model cards, and recognised benchmark studies, the models are examined under a common framework covering response quality, reasoning, coding, language understanding, context-window capacity, speed, computational requirements, cost, privacy, and deployment flexibility. No new experiments are conducted, and results obtained under different evaluation conditions are not treated as directly equivalent. The analysis shows that model selection involves trade-offs: hosted models offer easier access, whereas models with downloadable weights give greater deployment control but require more computing resources. No single model is found to be best for every task, which supports a task-specific approach to selecting LLMs.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models

organizations: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi;

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction

organizations: Department of Orthopedics, Taizhou People’s Hospital

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used by the public to obtain health information, but the safety and quality of their responses to questions about osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (OVCFs) remain unclear. Objective To compare the safety and patient-facing response quality of four publicly accessible LLM chatbots when responding to standardized questions about osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures. Methods In this cross-sectional paired evaluation, 36 standardized OVCF-related patient-facing questions were submitted to each of four publicly accessible LLM chatbot interfaces—ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Doubao—in an initial response-generation round on June 20, 2026, from Jiangsu, China. Queries were conducted in English in independent single-turn sessions under matched conditions, yielding 144 responses for the primary between-chatbot analysis. A second independent generation round using the same 36 questions and matched query procedures was conducted 7 days later (June 27, 2026), yielding an additional 144 responses for within-model stability analysis. The questions covered symptoms and warning signs, diagnosis and imaging, conservative management, medication safety, rehabilitation, vertebral augmentation, fracture prevention, and special clinical scenarios. Five clinical raters, blinded to chatbot identity and generation round, independently evaluated safety, factual accuracy, empathic communication, treatment-related information quality using DISCERN, patient-information quality using EQIP, transparency using the JAMA benchmark criteria, and overall quality using the Global Quality Score. Readability was assessed automatically using six established indices. Between-chatbot comparisons and test–retest stability analyses used paired methods appropriate for the outcome type.
evidence_items.title: Performance of four large language model chatbots in responding to patient-facing questions about osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: a cross-sectional paired evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Broadband coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (BCARS) enables label-free hyperspectral chemical imaging, but weak signal components are often obscured by heteroscedastic noise. Here, we develop a physics-based variance stabilization transform and benchmark six hyperspectral denoising methods to identify effective strategies for BCARS noise reduction. The transform yields nearly intensity-independent noise variance while preserving the dispersive Raman response. Within this framework, we compare singular value decomposition, BM4D, Noise2Noise, deep image prior, self-supervised diffusion, and a cross-covariance-based singular value decomposition method (CCV) introduced here, using a shared phase-retrieval pipeline. Evaluation includes five simulated hyperspectral cubes with exact ground truth and experimental measurements of glycerol, polystyrene beads, and Caenorhabditis elegans. In simulations, variance stabilization reduces the ratio of maximum to minimum channel noise variance from approximately 72 to 1.2. Deep image prior and self-supervised diffusion achieve the highest mean foreground peak signal-to-noise ratios. CCV matches the mean foreground structural similarity of deep image prior with substantially shorter runtime and no per-cube rank tuning. Experimental comparisons reveal sample-dependent performance. These results establish physics-based variance stabilization as a common framework for adapting and evaluating hyperspectral denoisers for BCARS, with CCV offering a practical balance of reconstruction fidelity, computational speed, and automated operation.
evidence_items.title: Denoising broadband CARS hyperspectral images on variance-stabilized data: a unified benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose The mechanical damage of red blood cells (hemolysis) remains a key challenge in the design of blood-contacting medical devices. This study aims to compare the predictive performance of the empirical power-law model and the physiologically motivated viscoelastic model in the FDA nozzle benchmark geometry, with a focus on how model parameters and shear stress definitions influence hemolysis predictions. Methods Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were performed using a finite volume framework to resolve flow fields and shear stresses in the FDA nozzle. Both hemolysis models were implemented under identical geometry, mesh and boundary conditions. A parametric analysis was conducted by varying key model parameters, including the viscoelastic constants A , $$T 1$$ T 1 , $$T 2$$ T 2 , the shear stress threshold $$\tau S$$ τ S , and the power-law parameters. Predictions were evaluated using both total shear stress and turbulent viscous shear stress (TVSS) formulations, and compared against experimental data. Conclusion The viscoelastic model demonstrated strong sensitivity to the relaxation time $$T 2$$ T 2 and to the choice of stress definition. A quasi-linear dependence on parameter A was identified, enabling calibration with experimental results. In contrast, the power-law model was less sensitive to stress definitions but strongly dependent on parameter fitting. The effect of $$\tau S$$ τ S differed between the two models: it reduced hemolysis in the power-law case but increased it in the viscoelastic formulation. Background The viscoelastic model offers a more mechanistic description of hemolysis but requires careful parameter calibration and is highly sensitive to stress definitions. The power-law model remains computationally efficient and easier to implement, though empirical by nature.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Power-Law and Viscoelastic Hemolysis Models in the FDA Nozzle Benchmark Geometry

organizations: Shanghai Key Laboratory of Maternal Fetal Medicine, Shanghai Institute of Maternal-Fetal Medicine and Gynecologic Oncology, Shanghai First Maternity and Infant Hospital, School of Medicine, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
evidence_items.summary: Background: The four molecular subtypes of endometrial carcinoma defined by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) can be reconstructed from multi-omics data, but these data contain about 460,000 features for 369 patients, the subtypes are imbalanced, and feature selection easily leaks test-set information. Methods: We developed POISE-X, a leakage-controlled, imbalance-aware benchmarking pipeline with an interchangeable metaheuristic search engine. Using RNA-seq, miRNA, DNA methylation, copy-number, mutation, and clinical data from 369 TCGA-UCEC patients, we compared 19 optimizers under nested five-fold cross-validation, with in-fold prefiltering to 2505 candidate features and a macro-averaged F1 fitness function. Results: Performance differed across optimizers in a Friedman test on fold means (p=1.989×10−6). No selected panel exceeded logistic regression on the full candidate pool, which reached a macro-averaged F1 of 0.902; the compact configuration chosen by our selection rule, POISE-GWO, retained 443 features with a macro-averaged F1 of 0.880, and the selection rule itself scored 0.881 under leave-one-fold-out evaluation, and an ANOVA-ranked panel of 450 features reached 0.886. These results held without clinical variables and, in the two searches tested, for parsimony weights of 0.8–0.99. A surrogate of the clinical molecular classification built from POLE exonuclease-domain mutation, mismatch-repair deficiency, and TP53 mutation reached a macro-averaged F1 of 0.924, higher on average than every multi-omics model. Conclusions: In this cohort, wrapper search therefore compressed the feature set without adding discriminative power, and the selected panels reconstructed an existing classification, not a new treatment-relevant signature. POISE-X is a framework for benchmarking feature-selection strategies; any selected panel requires external validation before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: A Leakage-Controlled Benchmark of Metaheuristic Multi-Omics Feature Selection for Reconstructing TCGA Molecular Subtypes in Endometrial Cancer

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Timely cause-of-death (COD) information guides health policy, yet many deaths in low- and middle-income countries are not medically certified. In Africa, fewer than 10% of deaths are. Verbal autopsy (VA) yields a structured symptom questionnaire and a free-text narrative. Mortality surveillance increasingly records the narrative alongside the questionnaire, but the algorithms used to produce VA-based statistics were designed for structured responses only, so narratives inform physician COD assignment but do not contribute to algorithmic COD assignment. We evaluated whether supervised models could use both modalities to improve COD assignment. METHODS We analyzed 4,999 VA records for deaths at ages 12 years or older from a national sample of registered deaths in South Africa (RSA), using physician-assigned CODs as the reference standard. We trained unimodal and multimodal pipelines on the labelled records: pretrained language models (PLMs) fine-tuned on narratives alone, machine learning (ML) models on structured responses alone, and the two combined at the data, feature, and decision levels. We also prompted a locally deployed generative large language model (LLM) on the same unimodal and multimodal inputs, without parameter updates. All were compared with InSilicoVA, the operational comparator representing current automated practice. We evaluated individual-level assignment, population-level agreement, calibration, and generalization across provinces in RSA, reporting these metrics rather than ranking pipelines on any one of them. RESULTS Every supervised pipeline improved on InSilicoVA by 8.5-15.9 percentage points in top-1 accuracy and 3.5-7.1 points in cause-specific mortality fraction (CSMF) accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Cause-of-Death Assignment From Verbal Autopsy Records: A National Benchmark Study in South Africa

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate ground-based cloud classification is important for atmospheric monitoring, solar-energy forecasting, aviation weather assessment, and climate observation systems. However, reliable sky-image annotation is time-consuming, especially when cloud types are visually similar or mixed. In this work, we study the label efficiency of deep learning for ground-based cloud classification using the Ground-based Cloud Dataset (GCD). Rather than proposing a new architecture, we benchmark three practical learning strategies under limited annotation budgets: supervised transfer learning, uncertainty-based active learning, and high-confidence pseudo-labeling. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 is used as a common frozen backbone, and experiments are repeated over five random seeds for label budgets ranging from \((1%)\) to \((100%)\) of the training labels. Supervised transfer learning is already highly label-efficient: test accuracy increases from \((0.635 \pm 0.018)\) with \((1%)\) labels to \((0.730 \pm 0.002)\) with \((40%)\) labels, approaching the full-label performance of \((0.735 \pm 0.003)\). Active learning and pseudo-labeling are competitive with supervised sampling and provide small improvements for some metrics and budgets, but neither produces a large or consistent aggregate gain. Diagnostic analyses show that accepted pseudo-labels are highly reliable, with accuracy ranging from \((0.946)\) to \((0.977)\), but are biased toward easier, high-confidence sky-type groups. In contrast, uncertainty sampling preferentially queries uncertain samples from visually challenging groups, including Mixed and the visually confusable Stratocumulus and Cumulonimbus groups, but these targeted acquisitions yield only modest performance improvements. Overall, these results show that transfer learning can substantially reduce annotation requirements for GCD, while simple active and semi-supervised strategies provide limited additional gains over a strong supervised baseline.
evidence_items.title: Label-Efficient Learning for Ground-Based Sky-Image Classification: A Benchmark of Transfer Learning, Active Learning, and Pseudo-Labeling on GCD

evidence_items.summary: An AI data center is committed years before it draws a watt: a few discrete choices (grid or on-site gas, evaporative or dry cooling, which county to file in) fix its capital, water draw, and carbon path, and LLMs are now asked to help screen them with no test of whether they track what each commitment rules out. We introduce DCBench-440, with two arms reported separately: 200 generative questions over STRIPS worlds for five US deal archetypes, with search-verified gold answers and no tested shortcut above 12% on any question type, and 240 multiple-choice questions grounded in quoted site records, emission equations, and stated scenarios. Across open-weight deployments, accuracy spans 12.5-71.5% (generative) and 58.3-92.5% (multiple choice). One skill fails everywhere: asked to list every action available at a decision gate, no model exceeds 4.0% exact match. The strongest list 72-85% of the actions that would change the project's state but omit most permitted actions that change nothing; with those excused, the best exact match is still 24%. Code, data, and other materials are available upon request.
evidence_items.title: Watts If? A Benchmark for Counterfactual Reasoning About the AI Data Center Buildout

evidence_items.summary: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.
evidence_items.title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.
evidence_items.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly store user preferences in persistent memory to support personalization across interactions. However, in third-party communication settings governed by social and institutional norms, some user preferences may be inappropriate to apply. We introduce BenchPreS, which evaluates whether memory-based user preferences are appropriately applied or suppressed across communication contexts. Using two complementary metrics, Misapplication Rate (MR) and Appropriate Application Rate (AAR), we find even frontier LLMs struggle to apply preferences in a context-sensitive manner. Models with stronger preference adherence exhibit higher rates of over-application, and neither reasoning capability nor prompt-based defenses fully resolve this issue. These results suggest current LLMs treat personalized preferences as globally enforceable rules rather than as context-dependent normative signals.
evidence_items.title: BenchPreS: A Benchmark for Context-Aware Personalized Preference Selectivity of Persistent-Memory LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language tasks but remain brittle in domains requiring precise logical and symbolic reasoning. Chaotic dynamical systems provide an especially demanding test because chaos is deterministic yet often misinterpreted as randomness or complexity. We introduce ChaosBench-Logic, a benchmark that evaluates LLM reasoning across 30 diverse dynamical systems using a unified first-order logic (FOL) ontology. Each system is annotated with truth assignments for 11 semantic predicates, and 621 questions are generated across seven reasoning categories, including multi-hop implications, cross-system analogies, counterfactual reasoning, bias probes, and multi-turn dialogues. We define metrics for logical accuracy, implication consistency, dialogue coherence, and contradiction, and we release an open-source evaluation pipeline. Initial experiments show that frontier LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and the open-source LLaMA-3 70B achieve 91-94% per-item accuracy, yet still score 0% on compositional items and exhibit fragile global coherence. Dialogue-level accuracy ranges from 53.1% (GPT-4 CoT) to 75.5% (LLaMA-3 zero-shot). ChaosBench-Logic provides a rigorous testbed for diagnosing such failures and a foundation for developing neuro-symbolic approaches that improve scientific reasoning in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: ChaosBench-Logic: A Benchmark for Logical and Symbolic Reasoning on Chaotic Dynamical Systems

evidence_items.summary: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

authors: Weihao Li, Zihang Xu, Zhongqiu Wang, Songwei Yu, Wenqiang Zhu, Yuechen Luo, Jingxuan Xu, Yanan Wu, Haoyang Huang, Ken Deng
evidence_items.summary: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.
evidence_items.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents

authors: Yijia Mao, Song Dai, Tao Chen, Xiangyu Lu, Linqian Zeng, Chenxi Hu, Sitong Zhou, Dongyang He, Xiaodan Mao, Linxuan Zhang, Tong Zhu, Yafu Li, Fangchen Yu, Peng Ye, Feng He, Yu Cheng, Yun Luo
evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question. A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs, where Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reaches RC4 in only 32.7% of attempts. Across the benchmark, 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fall short of RC4, while all seven models reach RC4 on substantially fewer tasks in all three runs than in at least one. Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure. Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.
evidence_items.title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research

authors: Zihao Zheng (Washington University in St. Louis), Junyi Yao (Washington University in St. Louis), Baichuan Li (Southern Methodist University), Jiayu Long (Washington University in St. Louis)
evidence_items.summary: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures

authors: Youran Sun, Xingyu Ren, Chugang Yi, Kejia Zhang, Di Wu, Yingkang Cao, Allen Zhou, Jianping Ye, Suying Liu, Jiaxuan Guo, Jianda Du, Weicheng Ye, Kecheng Liu, Hefan Zhang, Haixin Wang, Jie Xiao, Eric Yang, Haizhao Yang
evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$\Pi$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$\Pi$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: Sci$\Pi$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents

authors: Yakup Koray Budanaz, Lorenzo Paleari, Marcin Copik, Alexandru Calotoiu, Timo Schneider, Benjamin Chen Ming Choong, Shriram Chandran, Lars Hulsbergen, Levi Widmer, Torsten Hoefler
evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.
evidence_items.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.
evidence_items.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research

evidence_items.summary: Video subtitle removal (VSR) is an important video restoration task, yet existing evaluation remains limited by low-resolution datasets, fragmented test sets, and generic video-inpainting protocols that fail to adequately capture localized restoration errors, unintended modifications, temporal instability, and incomplete outputs. In this paper, we introduce MFVSR, a large-scale multi-style benchmark for fine-grained and reliability-aware video subtitle removal evaluation. MFVSR distinguishes itself through three key features: (1) Large-scale and diverse data, comprising 3,000 paired videos from Real-HQ, Real-LQ, and AI-Generated sources, with an auxiliary set of 953 in-the-wild real videos for real-world coverage analysis; (2) Controlled subtitle diversity, spanning 16 languages and four factors covering spatial layout, temporal behavior, visual style, and language mode; (3) Fine-grained evaluation, introducing an information-conditioned, spatially decoupled protocol that separates blind from mask-guided removal and measures Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, Temporal Fidelity, coverage, and failures. Experiments on six representative methods reveal substantial discrepancies between local restoration, outside-region preservation, temporal consistency, and full-set reliability that are obscured by conventional full-frame metrics. MFVSR therefore provides a more comprehensive and diagnostic foundation for evaluating and advancing video subtitle removal methods.
evidence_items.title: MFVSR: A Multi-Style and Fine-Grained Benchmark for Video Subtitle Removal

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Systematic reviews are the gold standard for evidence synthesis, but the manual title and abstract screening of thousands of references creates a severe bottleneck. Existing automated tools have historically struggled to achieve the near-perfect recall (sensitivity) required for reliable reviews. We developed MechaScreener as a ‘zero-shot’ automated screening tool that utilises a large language model to rank article relevance. The tool requires no initial training data or manual pre-screening, as MechaScreener directly applies user-provided question elements (PICO) or inclusion/exclusion criteria to assign an ordinal relevance score (1–5) to each reference. We evaluated the tool in two phases: a development phase using five reference libraries to optimise prompts, and an independent evaluation phase using 10 diverse Cochrane review libraries (comprising both randomised controlled trials [RCTs] and non-RCTs) containing over 58,000 references. In the evaluation dataset, MechaScreener achieved a perfect recall of 1.00 (100%) in all 10 reviews, ensuring that no relevant articles were missed (pooled record-level 95% CI: 0.98–1.00). Concurrently, it achieved an overall macro-average specificity of 0.61 (61%, cluster bootstrap 95% CI: 0.46–0.75; pooled record-level specificity 0.59, 95% CI: 0.59–0.60). Specificity varied from 0.21 in broad public health topics to 0.91 in precise pharmacological interventions, reflecting the tool’s built-in conservatism when evaluating ambiguous abstracts. By safely eliminating over 60% of irrelevant literature during the initial screening phase without compromising recall, MechaScreener functions as a highly reliable but low-effort ‘first-pass’ filter, allowing researchers to substantially reduce manual workloads and reallocate resources towards full-text review and data extraction.
evidence_items.title: MechaScreener: Large language model-based automated screening for systematic reviews and research

evidence_items.summary: Access to safe drinking water remains a global challenge, with approximately 2.1 billion people lacking safely managed water services. Continuous, low-cost monitoring of heavy metal contamination is limited because conventional techniques such as atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) are accurate but require centralized laboratories and high operational costs. Although machine learning has shown promise for water quality prediction, existing models are generally trained on empirical datasets and lack the physical constraints governing sensor behavior. This study addresses this limitation by developing a physics-informed machine learning framework based on a physically consistent synthetic dataset of 300 samples generated from Ohm's law, Kohlrausch's law of molar conductivity, and metal-hydrolysis pH chemistry. The dataset was utilized to predict heavy metal concentration from voltage, current, conductivity, temperature and pH. The Random Forest (RF) and Multi-Layer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models were benchmarked against linear regression using cross-validation of 5-folds and 10-folds. The ANN was optimized with L2 regularization and early stopping. During 5-fold cross-validation, the accuracy of RF was found to have R² of 0.38 ± 0.13 (RMSE = 0.049 ± 0.004 mg/L; MAE = 0.039 ± 0.003 mg/L), while ANN optimization was improved from R² = −0.05 till 0.22. Linear regression produced the best performance (R² = 0.47 ± 0.16), consistent with the predominantly linear physics underlying the dataset. Conductivity was identified as the dominant predictor, accounting for approximately 87% of RF feature importance and remaining robust under simulated sensor noise of up to 10%.
evidence_items.title: Physics Informed Machine Learning for Electrical Sensing and Prediction of Heavy Metal Contamination in Water

evidence_items.summary: In minoritized (low-resource) language technologies, a common response to data sparsity is to aggregate text across multiple varieties and treat the combined data as a single corpus. However, mixed corpora of closely related indigenous variants can produce an artificial register that is accountable to no single speaker community, a structural failure we call variant fragmentation. This issue is acute for minoritized languages native to Mexico, such as Nawatl. Building on a 70,000-pair multi-variant foundation, we specialize an mT5-large checkpoint to Masewalkopa (nhn), the Nawatl variety spoken in Santa Ana Tlacotenco. We curate 2,665 parallel pairs, reserve all sentence-level data for evaluation, and incorporate 192 elder-transcribed target sentences via asymmetric backtranslation. A custom finite-state analyzer reduces unanalyzed surface forms from 82.0% to 19.9% and supplies functional syntax tags as plain-text prefixes, allowing the model to reuse existing subword embeddings rather than relying on frozen special tokens. The resulting LoRA-v9c-b model achieves 58.46 dev chrF++ and 58.20/57.90 directional test chrF++. Finally, CTranslate2 int8 quantization reduces CPU latency from 137.5 to 1.8-2.6 seconds per request, enabling cost-bounded Cloud Run deployment.
evidence_items.title: Unfragmenting Nawatl NMT: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa

evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.
evidence_items.title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark scenarios, their generator, event records of every reported run, frozen memory engine, runners, and scoring and analysis scripts for the paper "Two-stage measurement of Update Adherence in language model memory agents" (submitted to PeerJ Computer Science). Update Adherence (UA) measures whether a revised requirement, and not the statement it replaced, governs the answer of a language model agent with external memory. It is scored at two stages using deterministic rules without a language-model judge, in the assembled context supplied to the answering model and in the generated answer. Tables 5 to 9, the values plotted in Figures 3 to 8, and the event breakdowns quoted in the Results can be recomputed from the released result files using python analysis/make tables.py. File integrity can be verified using python analysis/verify manifest.py. The command bash reproduce.sh performs both steps and additional consistency checks. All 84 scenario files can be regenerated and compared with the released copies using python generator/regenerate scenarios.py --output-dir DIR. Release v1.1 adds the scenario regeneration scripts, the derivation of the implicit-revision variants, a standard-library manifest check, and expanded documentation. No scenario, result, engine, or figure-data file has changed since v1.0, and MANIFEST.sha256 is unchanged. See CHANGELOG.md. Code is distributed under the MIT License. evidence_items.summary: AquaSense-ICS: a hybrid real-simulated cyber-physical dataset and leakage-aware benchmark for smart water quality monitoring and attack detection Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. AquaSense-ICS co-registers, on a common elapsed-time axis: Real edge recording: a 25.4 h window (8.0 h of recorded data, 31.5% coverage, 23 gaps longer than 60 s) from a Raspberry Pi 5 node with a TDS probe and a Bosch BME680 ambient sensor (temperature, relative humidity, gas resistance), sampled every 1-2 s (23,688 records). EPANET-MSX simulation: a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated for 24 h, with six water-quality species (chlorine, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, trihalomethanes) and one wall species, plus two pulse injections (chlorine at J3, turbidity at J7). Attack and fault library: a seeded generator of five cyber-attack types (false data injection, stealthy FDI, replay, denial of service, drift) and three unintentional sensor faults (white noise, spikes, extreme values), with sample-level ground truth. Augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, released in separate files and flagged by the origin column in the fused table. They are intended for training only. The accompanying paper also shows that random row splits combined with labels computed from the input features give near-perfect but uninformative scores, and defines a leakage-aware benchmark (chronological splits, held-out attack types).
evidence_items.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real–Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: We present Josh, a vegetation-focused platform for scalable ecological modeling. Co-developed in collaboration between research software engineers, ecologists, mathematicians, and land managers, this agent-based system aims to both further basic scientific understanding and support land management decisions. More specifically, this cross-disciplinary project centers the goals of both reducing the engineering effort required to author simulations and to offer strong performance in those models. Towards these ends, a domain-specific language (DSL) invites diverse collaborators to concisely specify custom logic for organisms and ergonomically access geospatial data as a first class language element. Then, with minimal to no code changes, this open source platform can use this DSL to move the same simulation from running locally in-browser via WebAssembly (WASM) to local parallelization via Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Finally, Josh can take the same code up to large scale distributed computing workloads. Through this portable computational machinery, the presented benchmark simulations not only require considerably less code compared to their expression in a comparable framework but they also run faster: the presented benchmarking task finds Josh requires an average 54% less wall clock time in "naive" solutions from large language model coding assistants (LLMs) and 15% less wall clock time in faster manually-optimized "expert" authored implementations. In either case, Josh is optionally compatible with Docker, Kubernetes, or similar. To support adoption of this platform, we also provide context-efficient techniques including MCP and llms.txt to facilitate AI assistance while building models. We test these features across multiple assistants from a range of providers. Altogether, this domain-specific platform seeks to offer concise and performant ecological models.
evidence_items.title: Josh: Efficient, Portable, and Scalable Cross-Disciplinary Vegetation Modeling via Domain-Specific Language

evidence_items.summary: © The Author(s) 2025.Background: A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) result ≥ 10 µg/g is recommended in the UK to triage patients with symptoms of colorectal cancer (CRC) in primary care for urgent cancer investigation. The COLOFIT model combining FIT results with demographics and blood tests was developed to reduce the proportion of people referred without CRC. This study aims to externally validate the COLOFIT using data from Oxford University Hospitals (OUH). Methods: FITs requested by GPs between January 2017 and February 2024 were extracted from the OUH Clinical Data warehouse. Adults with COLOFIT predictors and 180-day follow-up for CRC were included. External validation of the COLOFIT equation was conducted overall and for six independent time periods. Risk score thresholds where the model captured the same number of cancers as FIT ≥ 10 µg/g were estimated to understand the number of urgent referrals avoided. Results: A total of 51,477 individuals (659 CRC) were included; 6194 (12%) had FIT ≥ 10 µg/g. FIT positivity and testing volume increased over time, associated with a gradual change from testing lower-risk patients to including those with higher-risk symptoms. COLOFIT was poorly calibrated overall (observed/expected [O/E] ratio 1.52 with calibration slope 1.05), but calibration improved over time (up to O/E ratio 1.09 with calibration slope 1.05). COLOFIT reduced referrals by 8% overall without missing colorectal cancers compared to FIT ≥ 10 µg/g, but this varied from 23% reduction to 2% increase depending on the period evaluated. Conclusions: The potential benefit of COLOFIT varied depending on FIT testing rates, the proportion of FIT ≥ 10 µg/g, and the symptoms in the tested population. Adopting COLOFIT into current clinical practice demands, therefore, FIT positivity of at least 17% and CRC rates within 1.3–1.6%.
evidence_items.title: External validation of the COLOFIT colorectal cancer risk prediction model in the Oxford-FIT dataset: the importance of population characteristics and clinically relevant evaluation metrics

evidence_items.summary: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.
evidence_items.title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).
evidence_items.title: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning via Event-Centric Alignment

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agentic RL is constrained by the futures visited by the current policy. When rollouts fail to reach useful behaviors, improved credit assignment cannot provide supervision for states and actions that were never encountered. On-policy distillation (OPD) introduces teacher guidance on policy-induced states, and recent multi-turn variants improve how this guidance is scheduled, replayed, refined, or validated. However, they do not directly use the oracle-controlled future itself as the training trajectory. We introduce State-Rooted Executable Rollout Optimization (SERO), which augments on-policy agentic RL with executable oracle continuations. SERO restores a state actually reached by the current policy and lets a training-only oracle continue interacting with the real environment, making the downstream observations and oracle actions themselves available for learning. It then applies policy-reachability weighting, which weights each oracle step by the frozen behavior policy's compatibility with the preceding oracle actions. This allows deeper supervision to become effective as the policy becomes more compatible with the oracle branch. The oracle loss is optimized separately from the base RL estimator and no oracle is used at inference time. We evaluate SERO on two challenging interactive-agent benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. On ALFWorld, learning the full executable continuation is substantially more effective than supervising only the root oracle action, while policy-reachability weighting further improves out-of-distribution performance.
evidence_items.title: SERO: Learning from Executable Oracle Continuations for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: We present CommerceGen-Studio, an end-to-end framework for generating commercial-grade main images for e-commerce Stock Keeping Units (SKUs). Our framework is organized along a three-stage pipeline of information extraction, semantic rewriting, and multi-condition generation: Prompt-Eval-Refine-Loop Agent (PERL-Agent) distills heterogeneous SKU metadata into concise selling-point text lists through an iterative closed loop of VLM and LLM roles scored by a reference-free rubric. Layout Thinker Optimization (LTO) aligns the rewriter with both caption and rendered-image quality via alternating domain-specific policy optimization. SKU-DiT, trained under Reinforce-Distill-Reinforce (RDR) progressive training, conditions jointly on the white-background product image, the trademark crop, and the structured layout to hold subject fidelity, trademark integrity, and character-level text accuracy together. The framework runs in production at a scale of millions of main images per day with a latency of a few seconds per image, which we believe makes it among the first systems of this kind to operate at commercial scale. We also release CommerceGen-Bench, a benchmark of hard cases collected from live traffic across all product categories. On it, our framework achieves the highest overall scores among the evaluated open-source baselines on both editing tracks, with and without prompt enhancement. It also matches much larger closed-source models, and beats several of them at Instruction Following and Product Integration - the two properties that determine whether an image can be published.
evidence_items.title: CommerceGen-Studio: An End-to-End Framework for Commercial-Grade Main-Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.
evidence_items.title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?

evidence_items.summary: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale

evidence_items.summary: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.
evidence_items.title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.
evidence_items.title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Open-source web agents are now strong enough to execute realistic browser tasks, but training them with reinforcement learning still depends on weak supervision: binary task success is too sparse for credit assignment, while frontier-language-model judges are too expensive to call at every step and cannot be assumed available at deployment. We introduce CLIFT, a training and test-time scaling method built around conformal self-verification. During training, the agent answers natural-language verification questions about its own rollouts; a Compositional Conformal Certifier keeps only question signals whose URL-conditional evidence agrees with a training-time judge, assigns signed trust weights through polarity-aware lift, and blends the resulting verifier score into per-step rewards in a way that never subtracts from the judge baseline. At test time, the same certified bank is frozen and reused as structured evidence for Conformal Trajectory Selection (CTS): the agent samples a greedy rollout and one or more diverse retries, the self-verifier summarises each URL trace, and a conservative majority-vote rule chooses whether to swap away from the current incumbent without calling any external judge. This single mechanism supports three settings. On WebArena Infinity, CLIFT achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source web agents. On VisualWebArena, a bank trained with the open model transfers to GPT-5.5 at test time and reaches state-of-the-art performance under the canonical harness. On Online Mind2Web, without training an agent on the benchmark, translating the certified question bank improves a live-web agent in zero-shot evaluation. Together these results position conformal self-verification as a way to turn costly judge feedback into a reusable training signal and a judge-free test-time scaling signal.
evidence_items.title: CLIFT: Conformal Self-Verification for Web Agent Training and Test-Time Scaling

evidence_items.summary: Introduction. With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technology, large language models (LLMs) are expected to play an important role in improving access to and the use of library collections. This study constructs and develops a generative conversational large language model tailored specifically to epitaphs, overcoming traditional research paths and systems of digitisation. Method. Based on the Chinese epitaph database built by the Zhejiang University Library and some commercial epitaph databases, an epitaph generative dialogue large language model was constructed using Doubao as the base model through pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and other full process trainings. Analysis. This study used human evaluation, in which experts, researchers, or general users assessed the quality of model-generated outputs. The evaluation included the epitaphs of Cui Yi, Liu Yi, and Lihua in the Tang dynasty. Results. The model successfully performed intelligent interpretation of epitaphs, automatic information extraction, and other knowledge-based services, thereby providing new ideas for constructing an ancient literature corpus from excavated materials represented by epitaphs. Conclusion. A large-scale domain-specific foundational model tailored for library applications was successfully developed. The study offers innovative approaches for processing historical texts and suggests new directions for AI integration in library knowledge systems.
evidence_items.title: Building a domain-specific large language model for Chinese ancient books: a case study on epitaph modelling

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This chapter provides a foundational account of artificial intelligence for the book’s later analysis of key concepts of insurance and insurance law. It traces AI’s development from Turing and early expert systems to modern machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and general-purpose generative models, while distinguishing narrow AI, AGI, and ASI. It explains core AI techniques, the lifecycle of AI systems from data collection to post-deployment monitoring, and the main risks arising at each stage, including bias, opacity, hallucinations, security failures, deployment error, and feedback loops. The chapter also highlights the central role of data quality and governance, and surveys emerging standards and regulatory frameworks, particularly the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC standards, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Overall, it argues that understanding AI’s technical architecture is essential for assessing accountability, liability, and the evolving role of insurance in managing AI-related harms.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence: The Technology

evidence_items.summary: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data

organizations: Department of Cardiology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University; Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Fudan University;

evidence_items.summary: Background: Type-B aortic dissection requires separation of the true and false lumina in heterogeneous, anisotropic CTA. A topology term may reduce fragmentation, but its reproducibility must be tested under a fixed case split and independent native-grid evaluation. Methods: We used the public Graz type-B aortic dissection CTA collection (40 cases; CC BY 4.0) and froze a 28/6/6 case split for training, development, and held-out testing. A compact 2.5-D U-Net trained with cross-entropy plus multiclass Dice was compared with the identical model augmented by a fixed-weight (0.5) differentiable slice-level soft clDice term. Two training seeds were run for each arm. All 40 cases passed the NRRD audit; predictions for six held-out cases were restored to their native grids and scored with case-level 3-D voxel-grid Dice, voxel-grid morphological clDice, 6-connected component counts, physical-volume error, and 2,000-resample case-level paired bootstrap intervals. Results: With seed 20261007, topology-minus-baseline differences were -0.028 (95% CI -0.053 to -0.004) for true-lumen Dice, +0.032 (-0.006 to +0.096) for true-lumen voxel-grid clDice, +0.071 (+0.037 to +0.103) for false-lumen Dice, and +0.073 (+0.048 to +0.103) for false-lumen voxel-grid clDice. With seed 20261008, the corresponding differences were -0.040 (-0.065 to -0.018), +0.013 (-0.034 to +0.071), -0.099 (-0.187 to -0.004), and -0.058 (-0.124 to -0.001). Descriptive pooled means over 12 case rows per arm were true-lumen Dice 0.577 for topology versus 0.611 for baseline and false-lumen Dice 0.409 versus 0.422; these pooled rows are not independent cases. Conclusions: Under this fixed six-case test split, the corrected slice-level topology term did not produce a consistent benefit. True-lumen Dice was lower in both seeds, while false-lumen effects reversed direction between seeds; topology-clDice changes were small and/or interval-crossing.
evidence_items.title: A public-data reproducibility benchmark of a 2.5-D U-Net with a slice-level topology term for type-B aortic dissection segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reported accuracies on a widely used four-class brain tumor MRI benchmark routinely exceed 98%, but the released split discards patient identity. We content-matched tumor images to their figshare source and recovered identifiers for 4586 images from 233 patients. Of 906 tumor test images, 761 were traceable; every one belonged to a patient represented in training. Separately, 216 of 1311 test images were pixel-identical to training images. Removing duplicates did not reduce accuracy (99.22% to 99.42%), whereas five-fold patient-disjoint cross-validation yielded 95.19% overall and 93.68% on tumor classes. On the same 761 images, accuracy fell from 99.12% when the patient appeared in training to 93.60% when absent, increasing the error rate 7.3-fold. A matched random-fold control attributed 2.73 of the 4.03 percentage-point gap to patient grouping rather than the change in evaluation design; the class without patient identifiers changed negligibly despite relaxed proxy grouping. These results show that the released split measures recognition of additional slices from previously seen patients, not generalization to unseen patients. We release the recovered patient map, fixed folds, predictions, and analysis code.
evidence_items.title: Complete Patient-Level Leakage Among Traceable Images in a Widely Used Brain Tumor MRI Benchmark

organizations: Research Group of Advanced Control Systems, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Rambla Sant Nebridi 22, 08222 Terrassa, Spain
evidence_items.summary: Water-infrastructure digitalization increasingly couples hydraulics with sensing, communication, artificial intelligence (AI), and supervisory control, while digital twins support operational decisions. This article combines a critical narrative review with structured full-text evidence mapping of 50 water cyber-physical systems (CPS) studies and an accompanying reproducible Water Distribution Testbed (WDT) benchmark case study. The review synthesizes model-based, data-driven, and physically informed methods across detection, localization, mitigation, and recovery, distinguishing anomaly evidence, cyber attribution, and closed-loop resilience. The WDT case study compares nominal-only detectors and alarm policies under a common chronological protocol. Across five primary neural runs, cumulative policies increase sample-level recall but sustain alarms and detect fewer event onsets than the fixed-threshold policy. These numerical findings characterize the declared protocol and evaluated records; they do not establish a general ranking of detection algorithms. They motivate interpreting classification metrics alongside event performance and held-out nominal alarm burden. Priorities include trustworthy digital-twin updating, causal localization, uncertainty-aware intervention, independent validation, and verified recovery for intelligent water-infrastructure operation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twins, and Cyber-Resilience in Water Distribution Systems: A Critical Narrative Review with a WDT Benchmark Case Study

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This paper examines WebMCP, a proposed browser-native web platform standard that lets websites expose explicit, schema-described tools to large language model agents, as an alternative to actuation, in which an agent simulates the clicks, keystrokes, and navigation a human would perform. Methodology: The paper analyzes WebMCP, incubated within the World Wide Web Consortium's Web Machine Learning Community Group and implemented as an origin trial in the Chrome browser beginning with Chrome 149. We describe WebMCP's architecture, including the browser-mediated JavaScript interface navigator.modelContext and a declarative HTML annotation form, and its relationship to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol; analyze its security and permission model; place it within a comparative design-space taxonomy alongside DOM automation, computer-use agents, and server-side Model Context Protocol integrations; and examine the emerging standardization landscape, including browser vendor positions and adjacent efforts such as the Agentic Commerce Protocol. A generalized use case illustrates how a composite retail website might expose search, filtering, and checkout tools under this model. All sources and data referenced in this manuscript are dated on or before June 30, 2026. Findings: WebMCP allows a website to register tools that an agent invokes directly rather than inferring actions from pixels or DOM structure, with a security model built on origin isolation, a dedicated Permissions Policy directive, and a human-in-the-loop confirmation mechanism for consequential actions. Open problems remain in cross-site tool discovery, adversarial tool poisoning, and the evaluation of agent-web interaction quality. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper contributes a comparative design-space taxonomy that positions browser-native, declarative agent integration against actuation-based and server-side approaches.
evidence_items.title: WebMCP: A Browser-Native navigator.modelContext Standard for Agentic Web Automation

evidence_items.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information from large language models, but existing evaluations often measure forgetting only on a designated benchmark distribution. We argue that such behavioral forgetting is an insufficient standard for privacy-oriented unlearning, and that evaluation should instead test whether forgetting persists across the access paths through which the same information may be recovered. We demonstrate this with a controlled case study of cross-lingual querying: across multiple multilingual model families, forgetting varies substantially when semantically equivalent information is queried in different languages and scripts.
