evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?

evidence_items.summary: Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: $Q$ labeled questions and $N$ generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's infinite-generation voting rule. Under a margin condition with exponent $\beta$, we show that empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a calibrated margin buffer achieves excess risk of order $Q^{-1/2}+N^{-\beta/2}$, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed numbers of models and candidate answers. To investigate the optimality of this dependence on $Q$ and $N$, we analyze a simplified submodel with two models and two possible answers per question. We characterize its minimax excess risk up to constants by a Hellinger modulus for a binomial-mixture experiment. Polynomial approximation and spectral analysis reveal three regimes. When questions are relatively scarce, the $Q^{-1/2}$ term governs learning and the general buffered ERM is optimal. In an intermediate regime, pooling generation counts across questions improves upon estimating each answer distribution separately, with only logarithmic gains from additional questions. With sufficiently many questions, the minimax excess risk reaches an $N^{-\beta}$ identification floor that persists even with infinitely many questions. The submodel's lower bounds also apply to general ensembles, matching the buffered-ERM upper bound up to logarithmic factors when questions are scarce and in parts of the intermediate regime. Questions remain about the transitions between regimes and the construction of matching pooled estimators for general ensembles.
evidence_items.title: Two Sample Sizes in Test-Time LLM Ensembling: Buffered ERM and Minimax Theory

evidence_items.summary: Protein foundation models increasingly support the generation of novel biological sequences, yet their reliance on large public datasets creates opportunities for adversarial manipulation of the material they learn from and retrieve. We investigate two data-only poisoning attacks against protein design systems, targeting the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models and the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator. For the first, we pre-trained ProtGPT2 and ProGen2 variants of 300 million parameters, introducing poisoned protein sequences containing one of two triggers followed by one of three payloads. Across all poisoned runs, both architectures acquired highly reliable trigger-dependent generation under uniform and ramped poisoning schedules. Under ramped exposure, the earliest majority activation occurred after only 200 contaminated examples, while for the uniform schedule earliest activation occurred around 5000 poisoned samples. For the second attack, we inserted records into a retrieval corpus system without modifying its weights or decoding procedure. A single query-aware record captured a top-16 retrieval position for 58\% of templated requests and 97\% of free-text requests. Conditional on successful poisoned retrieval, 62\% of requests produced altered sequences, while 19-21% acquired the inserted domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal query-unaware attack using 1,500 records also achieved substantial retrieval capture and domain transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that adversarial protein sequence contributions can establish persistent, sequence-specific behaviour during pre-training or redirect protein generation at inference, while leaving ordinary model behaviour largely preserved. Our work establishes the integrity and biological provenance of protein sequence data as critical safeguards for generative protein design systems.
evidence_items.title: Poisoning the corpora of protein design systems during pre-training and retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Visible-light anti-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) detection is important for low-altitude UAV early warning by providing direct appearance and semantic cues. However, in fixed-viewpoint scenarios, UAV targets near the field-of-view (FOV) periphery often suffer from off-axis imaging degradation, which weakens local cues and hinders reliable detection. Existing approaches primarily focus on general small-target representation, whereas explicit modeling of FOV-peripheral degradation and weak-cue attenuation remains insufficient. To address this limitation, we propose WCMA-UAV, a wavelet-guided context modeling and aggregation network for fixed-viewpoint visible-light anti-UAV detection. WCMA-UAV is built around three coordinated components: the wavelet-coupled context module (WCCM), the hierarchical parallel aggregation unit (HPAU), and the progressive attention refinement head (PARH), forming a functional progression from degradation-aware feature extraction through structure-preserving aggregation to progressive refinement. Experiments on the DUT anti-UAV benchmark show that WCMA-UAV achieves the highest average precision (AP) among the compared detectors on both the official test set and the validation set, with the validation set containing a larger proportion of tiny UAV targets. These results indicate that WCMA-UAV improves weak-cue UAV detection near the FOV periphery.
evidence_items.title: Wavelet-Guided Context Modeling and Aggregation Network for Anti-UAV Detection

evidence_items.summary: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P<.05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P<.001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.
evidence_items.title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?

evidence_items.summary: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.
evidence_items.title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Data agents use code to process heterogeneous files and derive analytical insights. Scaling their training faces costly environment curation, privacy and intellectual-property restrictions, and difficulty verifying open-ended findings without known generative truth. Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. We introduce Data World, a multi-agent engine that synthesizes environments, tasks, and rubrics from explicit mechanisms. Independent audits check target recoverability from observed files; rubrics support evaluation and RL rewards. Human preference-based curation for question realism selects 100 tasks across 50 held-out worlds and 16 domains for DataWorld-Bench. The engine also yields 2,135 training tasks from 1,037 disjoint worlds. Evaluation of ten frontier models shows that the benchmark remains challenging, particularly for insight discovery, with a consistent computation-insight gap. RL-zero training on the synthesized tasks produces DataWorld-35B-A3B from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B without trajectory distillation. Under matched evaluation, it improves over its base by 7.06 points on DataWorld-Bench, 14.28 on DAComp, 20.90 on DABstep-Hard, and 12.13 on JobBench, a broader occupational benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch

evidence_items.summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness

evidence_items.summary: Computer use has reached a turning point: the focus is expanding from GUI-only interaction to systems that complete tasks on users' computers through visual and programmatic interfaces. We define a generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) as a system in which the model chooses how to observe, act, and organize its work across visual and programmatic interfaces. Yet frontier implementations, such as GPT-6 Astra's computer-use system, remain largely closed, limiting systematic study of their design. We introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for GCUAs with the community. This report presents the first release of OpenGCUA. Code execution is a key feature of our agent design: it lets intermediate results determine subsequent operations and enables models to apply their existing programming capabilities directly to computer interaction. We also propose harness-to-model decision transfer, moving selected observations and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On OSWorld-v2, our full configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, raising mean partial score by +19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. We release our implementation and prompts, evaluation trajectories from all eight models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The harness addresses real-device challenges not fully captured by benchmarks, while the SDK provides a common programming interface across computers, mobiles and browsers. Across four real macOS tasks under our real-device harness, selected Qwen3.8-Max runs use 19.4 times as many reported reasoning tokens as GPT-6 Astra, highlighting substantial differences between models in real-device execution efficiency.
evidence_items.title: OpenGCUA: Toward a Fully Open Stack for Generalist Computer Use

evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.
evidence_items.title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-Δ, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-Δ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms π_{0.5} in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
evidence_items.title: VLA-Δ: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
evidence_items.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms

evidence_items.summary: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.
evidence_items.title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling

evidence_items.summary: As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real-world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic prompting, often failing to capture the authentic, complex mechanics of software failures. To exponentially scale SWE task production, we introduce SWE-at-Scale, a framework that automatically synthesizes realistic issues by reverse-engineering real-world software fixes. Our key insight is that historical fixes encapsulate deep mechanistic knowledge of bug formation: inverting a fix transforms repair supervision into bug-induction supervision grounded in actual development scenarios. SWE-at-Scale transfers these learned bug patterns to novel code contexts, repeatedly sampling diverse bug typologies to construct executable SWE tasks. Extensive experiments show that SWE-at-Scale generates more diverse and realistic SWE tasks than current synthesis baselines while posing greater challenges to state-of-the-art coding agents. Notably, SWE-at-Scale can generate distinct bug types from a single code context, with bug diversity scaling robustly even up to 200 generations per file. Overall, SWE-at-Scale turns finite real-world fixes into reusable supervision for scalable synthesis of realistic, diverse, and challenging SWE tasks.
evidence_items.title: SWE-at-Scale: Scalable Issue Synthesis from Historical Bug Fixes

evidence_items.summary: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.
evidence_items.title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
evidence_items.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
evidence_items.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment

evidence_items.summary: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/
evidence_items.title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views

evidence_items.summary: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.
evidence_items.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness

evidence_items.summary: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.
evidence_items.title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.
evidence_items.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR

evidence_items.summary: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.
evidence_items.title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing

evidence_items.summary:
Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
  We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments

evidence_items.summary: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets. Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing
evidence_items.title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Fluorescence imaging in the second near‐infrared window (NIR‐II, 1000–1700 nm) has attracted increasing attention in biomedical applications owing to its deep tissue penetration, high spatial resolution, and low background autofluorescence. However, the rational optimization of high‐performance NIR‐II fluorophores remains challenging because of the complex relationship between molecular structure and optical properties. In this study, we integrated existing fluorescence datasets with NIR‐II fluorophore data to construct a comprehensive dataset covering maximum emission wavelengths from the visible region to the NIR‐II window. Based on this dataset, we developed a large language model (LLM)‐based framework for predicting molecular maximum emission wavelengths and compared its performance with conventional machine learning and deep learning models. The results demonstrated that the LLM achieved competitive predictive performance compared with the baseline models, highlighting the feasibility of LLM‐based structure–property prediction for fluorescent molecules. Model‐guided virtual screening was subsequently performed to prioritize candidate NIR‐II fluorophores, leading to the identification of two promising candidates that were experimentally characterized and exhibited favorable imaging performance in vitro and in vivo. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of LLM‐assisted structure–property prediction and virtual screening for NIR‐II fluorophores, providing an efficient computational strategy for candidate prioritization and molecular optimization.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model‐Assisted Prediction and Virtual Screening of Near‐Infrared‐II Fluorescent Molecules
A Benchmark of Small Language Models for Local Text-to-SQL over SQLite

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Regulatory frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Common Rule, and the Declaration of Helsinki require informed consent to ensure participants understand a study’s purpose and can make voluntary decisions about their involvement. Regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation [EU] 2016/679), further emphasize that consent must be freely given and revocable without disadvantage. Although informed consent forms (ICFs) are intended to be clear and accessible, they have become increasingly lengthy and complex. Large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to navigate and interpret this complexity and have shown promise in biomedical information extraction tasks. However, their susceptibility to hallucinations limits their reliability in high-stakes settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can mitigate such errors. Objective This study evaluates the integration of GPT-4.1 with RAG for reviewing data reuse language in ICFs and its ability to interpret complex ICF language. Methods First, we processed 438 ICFs from different trials, including multiple countries, languages, and versions of ICFs. Using expertly curated prompts, we extracted information about data reuse using GPT-4.1. By comparing the LLM-generated data reuse outputs with human expert ground truth, we evaluated accuracy and the time required to extract information for each ICF. To further validate the workflow, we evaluated an independent set of 488 ICFs spanning additional trials, languages, and regions. During the validation phase, the workflow was evaluated using a baseline assessment (89 ICFs) followed by 3 iterative optimization rounds assessed on 14, 281, and 104 ICFs, respectively. For this cohort, we assessed the correctness of LLM outputs along with the quality of supporting evidence provided by the model. Results Across the initial set of 438 ICFs, the system achieved 81.6% accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Review of Clinical Trial Informed Consent for Data Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to quantify psychological constructs from natural language, yet their outputs are typically evaluated only as predictions of an external label. When that label is itself imperfect, optimizing prediction conflates label agreement with construct measurement. No study has applied a multidomain measurement-oriented evaluation to LLM-derived psychological outputs. Objective We applied 5 psychometric evaluation domains to LLM-derived outputs to test whether measurement-oriented evaluation surfaces properties that prediction-oriented evaluation does not: extraction repeatability, convergent validity with a lexicon-based tool, ecological concurrent validity decomposed into within-person and between-person components, incremental value in a 4-arm comparison with that tool, and method-blinded expert evaluation with structured error attribution. Methods Thirteen linguistic features were extracted by GPT-5.2 (OpenAI) from 3556 person-days of daily voice narratives collected from 279 call center workers over 15 days via ecological momentary assessment. Features were evaluated across the 5 domains, with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, version 22, as the lexicon-based comparator. Multimodel robustness was assessed by re-extracting all features with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash. Results Features showed high repeatability (mean intraclass correlation coefficient=0.987), construct-dependent convergent validity (Spearman ρ=0.08 to 0.79), and within-person tracking of same-day stress (negative emotion β=0.68). In a 4-arm comparison (baseline, baseline plus lexicon features, baseline plus LLM-derived features, and baseline plus both), LLM features increased explained variance in daily stress from 13.2% to 30.4%, versus 16.9% for the lexicon-based comparator. Among transcripts sampled for maximal method discordance, experts preferred LLM-derived profiles in 83.7% (261/312) of blinded decisions.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Model–Derived Outputs as Psychological Measures: A Five-Domain Psychometric Framework With Application to Daily Stress

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate dietary advice, but their alignment with country-specific nutritional guidance remains uncertain. Aim To descriptively evaluate the alignment of the first seven-day meal plans generated by five publicly accessible LLMs with the Türkiye Dietary Guidelines (TÜBER) 2022 reference values for a 2000-kcal diet. Methods GPT-5.3 (ChatGPT), Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 4.2, the default free-web Microsoft Copilot model, and DeepSeek-V3 received an identical Turkish-language prompt describing a standardized healthy adult. Each model's first seven-day plan was analysed using nutrition analysis software. Percentage deviations from TÜBER references, Dietary Diversity Score and Food Variety Score were calculated and evaluated descriptively. Summary All plans had high dietary diversity. Mean energy ranged from 1378 to 1696 kcal/day, below the 2002-kcal reference. Fibre ranged from 23.3 to 33.5 g/day versus the 35-g reference, and riboflavin ranged from 1.43 to 2.19 mg/day versus 2.4 mg. Sodium ranged from 1759 to 2938 mg/day, exceeding the 1549-mg reference, whereas calcium ranged from 712 to 1032 mg/day versus 1284 mg. Deviations varied across plans, and no model was consistently closest to the references across all nutritional components. High dietary diversity did not ensure alignment with national nutrient reference values. LLM-generated meal plans require verification against national guidance and professional review before individualized use.
evidence_items.title: Alignment of large language model–generated meal plans with national nutrient reference values: A comparative analysis of five models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) aims to answer natural language questions by grounding them in structured knowledge graphs (KGs). Current KGQA systems still face three linked challenges: representing complex and compositional questions, providing transparent multi-hop reasoning traces, and using complete path-level evidence rather than only local triples. We propose SK-DRP ( S yntax- K nowledge enhanced D ynamic R easoning with P rompt learning), a modular KGQA framework that combines syntax-aware representation, state-adaptive path reasoning, and LLM-assisted answer selection. The syntax- and knowledge-enhanced encoder is an auxiliary representation enhancement that uses dependency information and knowledge-augmented pre-training to align questions with KG entities and relations. Here, dynamic denotes hop-wise recomputation of the question-focus indicator, score-qualified frontier expansion, and hop-weighted answer aggregation within a fixed dataset-level maximum hop budget; it does not denote automatic per-question depth selection. Candidate global paths are then compressed and transformed into natural-language auxiliary evidence for candidate-set-guided LLM answer selection. Experiments on MetaQA, WebQSP, and CWQ show that SK-DRP improves over several path-based and retrieval-based baselines on WebQSP and CWQ, while remaining competitive on MetaQA. Ablation, error, and interpretability analyses clarify how the syntax encoder, dynamic reasoning module, and LLM-assisted answer selection contribute to the final results, as well as the scope and limitations of the approach.
evidence_items.title: Dynamic path reasoning with large language models for interpretable knowledge graph question answering

organizations: The Shennong Laboratory, College of Animal Science and Technology Henan Agricultural University  Zhengzhou China
GeneMind Biosciences Company Limited  Shenzhen China
Agricultural Genomics Institute at Shenzhen Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences  Shenzhen China
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate and scalable evaluation of gene‐editing efficiency is crucial for the development of novel editing tools. However, conventional methods are laborious, costly, and low‐throughput. Here, we developed an artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven fluorescent reporter (AR) platform, an integrated system that automates and streamlines the entire evaluation workflow. The AR platform combines an enhanced fluorescent reporter with an AI‐driven analytical pipeline. The dual‐fluorescence reporter system, in which mCherry carrying a PEST domain is paired with GFP, supports Cas variants with diverse PAM requirements and quantifies editing efficiency as the proportion of GFP‐only cells. The platform's AI module, EasyReporter, integrates a deep learning model for automated cell segmentation and quantification with a large language model (LLM)‐based agent for intelligent data interpretation and comprehensive report generation. Editing efficiencies measured by AR correlated with those measured by flow cytometry (Spearman ρ = 0.77) and amplicon sequencing (Spearman ρ = 0.83). The AR platform provides a high‐throughput and automated workflow that accelerates gene‐editing research. In the future, it will be particularly effective for quantifying the efficiency of large‐fragment gene editing, offering a new framework for AI‐empowered biological laboratories.
evidence_items.title: AR: An Artificial Intelligence‐Driven Fluorescent Reporter System for Gene Editing Evaluation

authors: Hamad Ali M. A. Al Sowaidi
evidence_items.summary: This research investigates the deepest and most decisive layer of digital sovereignty: Artificial Intelligence, focusing on foundational models, computational power, and hardware infrastructure. By analyzing the State of Qatar’s strategic transition from a technological consumer to a producer—manifested in the national AI model “Fanar” and the establishment of the “QAI” company—the study explores the boundaries of strategic independence for small states. While Qatar has successfully secured a genuine sovereign asset through developing massive, culturally contextualized Arabic datasets that address structural linguistic gaps, critical analysis reveals a profound dependency on foreign foundational models and cloud architectures. The research further delves into the geopolitics of semiconductors, illustrating how hardware monopolies and export controls act as a rigid ceiling to absolute sovereignty, increasingly weaponized within the US-China technological rivalry. Consequently, the study reconceptualizes digital sovereignty for small states not as absolute autarky, but as a dynamic spectrum of “managed dependency.” To navigate this unequal global technological order, the state of Qatar must employ strategic multilateral partnerships, leverage open-source architectures, and capitalize on their sovereign wealth to mitigate vulnerabilities. Ultimately, a small state’s digital sovereignty is measured by its capacity to manage these dependencies, protect its socio-cultural specificity, and maximize its geopolitical margin of maneuver within entrenched structural constraints.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Sovereignty and Technological Dependency

evidence_items.summary: The digital ministerial practices of congregations have rapidly developed over the past few years, especially because of the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic. Many congregations accepted these challenges and used communication technology and social media, with valuable contributions to innovative ministerial practices. This quest is; however, recently further amplified by the rapid development and implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in various spheres of communal life. The question has now become a reflection on how congregations are functioning in an AI-informed world. On the one hand, as a space for worshipping and faith renewal; on the other hand, as a workplace that cannot be ignorant of the emerging AI-informed world. Comparing the perspectives of leading inter-disciplinary theorists with insights from an empirical enquiry, possible modalities for the interaction of faith communities with an AI-informed world are identified. Sprouting from these perspectives, the contribution reflects on the future development and interaction between congregational culture and an AI-informed world, providing critical evaluative thoughts on some concrete examples from current ministerial practices.
evidence_items.title: Congregations in an Artificial Intelligence-Informed World

organizations: Department of Master of Computer Applications  ASM’s Institute of Business Management & Research, Pune, Maharashtra, India
evidence_items.summary: With the growing use of digital images in online communication and social media, verifying whether an image is authentic has become increasingly important. Image manipulation techniques such as copy-move, splicing, inpainting, and object removal can change the meaning of visual information. At the same time, JPEG compression and repeated recompression can weaken the forensic traces that are useful for detection. This review looks at two AI-based approaches for detecting digital image forgery. The first study combines Error Level Analysis (ELA) with the VGG-16 convolutional neural network to classify images as original or tampered. The second study focuses on compressed images shared through social networks and uses a modified ShuffleNet V2 architecture for lightweight forgery classification. The two studies are reviewed based on their objectives, datasets, preprocessing or feature representation, deep learning architecture, compression conditions, findings, and limitations. The comparison shows that ELA with VGG-16 can help expose compression-related manipulation artifacts, while the modified ShuffleNet V2 approach focuses on the practical challenge of detecting forgery after JPEG and social-network recompression. The review highlights dataset diversity, compression robustness, computational efficiency, and generalization across different manipulation and sharing conditions as important research gaps. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Image Forgery, Deep Learning, Error Level Analysis, VGG-16,ShuffleNet V2, Image Compression.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Digital Image Forgery Detection

organizations: School of Nursing Hunan Normal University  Changsha Hunan China
School of Nursing Changsha Medical University  Changsha China
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Aims To examine the interconnections among artificial intelligence literacy, self‐regulated learning strategies, and academic resilience in undergraduate nursing students, and to conduct an exploratory comparison of network characteristics between students with and without clinical practice experience. Design A cross‐sectional survey. Methods Using convenience sampling, 1784 undergraduate nursing students were recruited from five universities in Hunan Province, China, between March and May 2026. Participants completed a demographic questionnaire and three validated scales. Network analysis estimated node strength, bridge strength, and predictability. Bootstrap procedures assessed network accuracy and stability, and the Network Comparison Test was used to conduct an exploratory comparison between students with and without clinical practice experience. Results The 10‐node network contained 35 non‐zero edges and had a mean predictability of 62.6%. Artificial intelligence evaluation showed the highest node strength, followed jointly by monitoring learning strategies and cognitive maturity. Evaluating and revising learning strategies showed the highest bridge strength, followed by cognitive maturity. In the exploratory subgroup analysis, the overall network structure differed between students with and without clinical practice experience, whereas global strength did not. Conclusions Artificial intelligence evaluation, monitoring learning strategies and cognitive maturity showed relatively high node strength, whereas evaluating and revising learning strategies and cognitive maturity showed relatively high cross‐domain bridge strength. Implications for the Profession Findings may inform nursing curricula integrating artificial intelligence literacy, learning regulation, and academic adaptation. Impact This study addressed fragmented understanding of these capacities.
evidence_items.title: Learning Adaptation in Artificial Intelligence‐Enabled Nursing Education: A Network Analysis of Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Self‐Regulated Learning and Academic Resilience

organizations: Department of Pharmacology and Biochemistry, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, USA.
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming how scientific hypotheses are formulated, tested, and applied. Nucleic acid therapeutics can benefit from emerging opportunities but will also face new challenges. AI lowers the barrier to hypothesis generation, increasing the emphasis on critical evaluation, rigorous experimental testing, and expert judgement. The goal of this perspective is to begin that discussion, with an emphasis on basic and applied research at the interface of nucleic acid science and medicine.
evidence_items.title: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in an Age of Artificial Intelligence
AuditLegalQA: A Benchmark for Legal Grounding in Public-Sector Audit Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Distributed and quasi-distributed optical fiber sensors (OFS) are deployed for structural health monitoring (SHM) of structures, yet their accuracy near sub-centimetre stress concentration areas remains uncertain. Three centimetre-scale sensing technologies are benchmarked against finite element method (FEM) predictions: fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs) in wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), continuous fiber gratings (CFGs) in frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW), and optical frequency-domain reflectometry (OFDR) under high strain gradients (HSGs) reaching around 200 µε mm−1. HSGs are generated in a 2 mm thick aluminium plate (80 × 765 mm2) with three holes (diameters Φ = 30 mm, 40 mm and 50 mm) loaded up to 2200 N by steps of 200 N. Gage-length averaging is the dominant error mechanism at the 40 mm and 30 mm holes when compared with the FEM structural benchmark: an 8 mm type-I FBG underestimates the FEM peak by 24 % and 30 %, respectively, while a 3 mm type-III FBG reduces this to around 10 % to 15 %. At the 50 mm hole, FBG type-III remains below FEM by about 12 % (1941 µε vs 2209 µε at 2000 N); at 1000 N, FEM, OFDR, and FMCW peaks are 1113.4 µε, 1332.25 µε (+20 %), and 555.4 µε (-50 %), respectively. OFDR requires moving-reference processing above 1600 N to prevent correlation breakdown. The relative accuracy of the 2 mm and 9 mm CFG-FMCW configurations varies with hole size and depends on gage overlap fraction; FMCW damping or spectral distortion occurs in high-gradient regions and is consistent with gradient-dependent spectral distortion, potentially involving chirp and proprietary peak-detection processing. These results provide guidance for sensor selection, gage-length specification, and signal-processing choices in SHM deployments where damage-induced strain concentrations are expected.
evidence_items.title: Optical fiber sensing under high strain gradients: a multi-technology benchmark against finite element predictions
MineClaim: A Benchmark for LLM-Based ESG Claim Verification and Greenwashing Detection in Australian Mining Reports

organizations: Facultad de Ciencias Humanas, Corporación Universitaria Minuto de Dios—UNIMINUTO, Bogotá 111021, Colombia
Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad Distrital Francisco José de Caldas, Bogotá 111711, Colombia
Universidad Distrital Francisco José de Caldas
evidence_items.summary: Nutritional estimation pipelines built on large language models are entering biomarker research, but free-text meal descriptions have no ground truth, so outputs cannot be validated against a reference standard. What can be established without one is whether the same input returns the same number. We submitted 191 de-identified Spanish meal descriptions, byte-identically, three times each, at temperature 0, to 20 model configurations across two inference platforms (12,119 calls), and measured test–retest reliability by ICC(1,1), cross-model agreement, internal Atwater coherence between reported energy and macronutrients, and the reliability gradient across input specificity. All 20 models exceeded the audited cascade’s energy ICC under both comparators, but reproducibility did not imply internal coherence: the most reproducible model (ICC 1.0000) departed from its own macronutrients by more than 10% under the simplified 4/4/9 Atwater approximation in 65.58% of responses, against 3.80% for the cascade. The two axes are close to orthogonal, and the dissociation needs no threshold to state: that configuration ranks first of 20 in reliability and first of 20 in incoherence at every bound between 5% and 20%. A binary acceptance gate is not robust to that bound—3 to 17 of 20 configurations pass across the range—whereas the ordering is (Kendall tau ≥ 0.74 between any two), so coherence is reported as a ranked screening dimension with a decision curve, not as a validated criterion. Test–retest reliability is therefore necessary but not sufficient to authorise an LLM-assisted nutritional pipeline, and acceptance requires at least one reference standard-free coherence check alongside the reliability estimate.
evidence_items.title: Reproducible but Incoherent: A Reference Standard-Free Reliability Benchmark of LLM-Assisted Nutritional Estimation Across 20 Model Configurations

organizations: Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Applied Sciences Münster, 48565 Steinfurt, Germany
West Central Research and Outreach Center, University of Minnesota, Morris, MN 56267, USA

evidence_items.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are persistent contaminants detected in groundwater at closed municipal landfills in rural Minnesota, where legacy waste continues to release PFASs decades after closure. In this setting, contaminated groundwater used for irrigation creates a direct pathway for PFAS transfer into the food supply. This study evaluates remediation at the groundwater–irrigation interface through a unified techno-economic assessment comparing granular activated carbon (GAC) adsorption and phytoremediation with Festuca rubra (F. rubra). Design influent concentrations were set at the 90th percentile (P90) of five representative PFASs measured in rural Minnesota landfill groundwater. Adsorption was simulated using a pore and surface diffusion model for single-bed and lead–lag configurations under fouling and non-fouling conditions. Phytoremediation was modeled using three complementary scenarios: a greenhouse-derived upper bound, a bioconcentration factor (BCF)-derived mechanistic case, and a decomposed scaling formulation. Unit costs were anchored to Minnesota Pollution Control Agency 2023 guidance and University of Minnesota (UMN) Extension data. Adsorption achieved compliance within weeks at $5.24–$8.00 m−3; phytoremediation showed lower per-volume cost ($0.43 m−3) but required centuries to multi-millennial timescales for long-chain PFASs. Cumulative cost was dominated by treatment duration rather than per-volume intensity, with adsorption more cost-effective when compliance timeframes are constrained. These findings highlight that remediation feasibility depends on alignment between treatment timescale and risk-management objectives rather than levelized cost alone.
evidence_items.title: Techno-Economic Assessment of Treatment Methods to Remediate PFAS Contamination in Leachate of Closed Landfills in Rural Minnesota

evidence_items.summary: Virtual reality enables studying active visual search and gaze behavior under naturalistic, free-viewing conditions while preserving experimental control. However, free head-eye coordination, extended 3D space, dynamic target trajectories, and headset-specific field of view and eye-tracking constraints mean that findings from traditional 2D paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to immersive environments. Interpreting gaze-based outcomes in VR requires bench-marks that establish how basic target properties influence detection. We used target eccentricity, size, and speed as benchmark predictors of visual detection in an immersive VR coin-foraging task. Using in-headset eye-tracking, participants guided a gaze-controlled avatar to collect coins that varied in gaze-relative eccentricity, size, and speed. We modeled gaze-based observation probability, observation latency, dwell time, gaze-coin angular distance, and saccade dynamics. Observation probability was analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression, whereas latency was analyzed with a censoring-aware Cox framework that retained never-detected coins. Eccen-tricity and size showed the clearest benchmark effects. Peripheral and small coins were less like-ly to be detected. Speed’s role was more nuanced. Although slow coins were detected more of-ten in a binary model, this advantage did not persist in a censoring-aware survival analysis, suggesting that speed influenced the opportunity for observation more than momentary salience. Consistent with this interpretation, slow coins produced longer dwell times, and gaze-coin an-gular distance and saccade measures indicated that target properties shaped both the geometry and effort for acquisition. These findings establish a feature-based benchmark for gaze-based de-tection in immersive visual search and demonstrate the importance of modeling missed targets as censored detection opportunities.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Gaze-Based Target Detection in Immersive Virtual Reality: Effects of Eccentricity, Size, and Speed on Observation and Detection Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics (MD) is increasingly used to study organic peroxide decomposition, although the parameter sets supplied with common MD codes were developed for other chemistries. We benchmarked the six C/H/O ReaxFF parameter sets distributed with LAMMPS against CBS-APNO O–O bond dissociation enthalpies (BDEs) of 13 peroxides and tested whether the static error carries over to the kinetics. All six sets underestimate the O–O BDE (mean signed errors of −11.9 to −30.5 kcal mol-1) and correlate only weakly with the references (r = 0.14–0.50). The newer CHO-2016 set (not distributed with LAMMPS) gives −19.5 kcal mol-1, whereas the same protocol yields 85–90 kcal mol-1 for the ethane C–C bond (experiment, about 90 kcal mol-1). The errors increase with alkyl and acyl substitution. For di-tert-butyl peroxide (DTBP), the sets predict 0.4–16.7 instead of 42.4 kcal mol-1, four of them stretch the O–O bond to 1.68–1.76 Å, and a fifth breaks it. Isothermal MD of DTBP at 575–1480 K with three sets gave activation energies of 45.0–76.5 kJ mol-1, consistent with each set’s static BDE (48.7–69.9 kJ mol-1) but 2.0–3.4 times lower than the experimental 153 kJ mol-1. At 121 °C, the extrapolated rate constants exceed manufacturer data by factors of 3.4 × 108 to 5.0 × 1012, and the predicted 10 h half-life temperatures (−147 to −59 °C) lie 180–270 °C below the measured 121 °C. Calculating the O–O BDE of the target peroxide is therefore a simple but necessary check before using a ReaxFF parameter set for hazard assessment.
evidence_items.title: Off-the-Shelf ReaxFF Parameter Sets Underestimate O–O Bond Strengths in Organic Peroxides: A Static and Kinetic Benchmark for Thermal-Hazard Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Visual generation is becoming a general component of AI infrastructure, supporting content creation across design, entertainment, education, science, and industry. Generative and multimodal models have substantially improved single-pass synthesis. At the same time, multi-step visual creation requires spatial precision, identity persistence, temporal coherence, editable structure, factual fidelity, and physical plausibility throughout the creation process. Errors in intermediate artifacts can propagate across subsequent steps, making creation control a central requirement. Model scaling, prompt refinement, additional conditioning, and repeated sampling improve individual outputs; coordinating these capabilities across a task requires runtime evidence to influence subsequent creation decisions. Within AI-generated content (AIGC), we use Agentic AIGC to describe goal-driven content creation organized through a multi-step control loop. This survey focuses on visual generation agents: systems that use runtime evidence from evolving visual artifacts, task environments, and interaction histories to change later creation-relevant action selection or parameterization, including generation, editing, verification, recovery, replanning, and stopping. The defining behavioral property is therefore an observation--action dependency: runtime observations change later action selection. Whether those decisions improve task or constraint outcomes is evaluated separately with matched tools and resource budgets. We organize this emerging field around the control mechanisms and behavioral evidence that connect generative capabilities to autonomous visual creation. Specifically, we formalize this boundary and characterize autonomy through five cumulative levels (L1--L5).
evidence_items.title: Agentic AIGC: A Survey of Visual Generation Agents

evidence_items.summary: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models'tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.
evidence_items.title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing

evidence_items.summary: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.
evidence_items.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents

evidence_items.summary: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
evidence_items.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Language models are often asked to make judgments: whether a proposed answer is correct, whether one statement follows logically from another, or whether a response is safe. Yet changing the instructions that specify how the judgment should be expressed can make the final answer less reliable, even for the same input. We ask whether this reflects a change in internal judgment or a failure to express it. Comparing hidden-state vectors for the same input under different instructions, we find that their differences concentrate in a low-dimensional expression subspace. We identify this subspace without benchmark labels and remove its contribution from a linear predictor to obtain an isolated judgment. Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment remains reliable under instructions not used to identify the subspace, even when the model's final answer and the original predictor degrade. When the judgment question is negated, isolation raises the predictor's AUROC from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety. We also find that judgment is readable in earlier layers, before the expression subspace begins to disrupt the predictor. Together, these results provide a way to separate judgment from expression and recover internal judgments even when the model's final answers are unreliable.
