Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.
evidence_items.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files

evidence_items.summary: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World

evidence_items.summary: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.
evidence_items.title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Vision--language pre-training has enabled substantial progress in image--text retrieval and zero-shot recognition by learning transferable cross-modal representations. However, sentence-level alignment remains insufficient for compositional matching, where captions can describe the same objects and attributes while differing in how these elements are bound. To address this limitation, we propose Flow-CLIP, which refines global image-text alignment through image-conditioned changes in token--patch evidence. Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) learns a sentence-level similarity metric, while Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) incorporates visual patch context into token queries and uses the resulting change in local matching evidence to adjust the global score. We further introduce Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR), which compares the same positive--negative caption pair across matched and mismatched images, encouraging a larger ranking margin when the image supports the correct description. Experiments on compositional matching and attribute--object binding benchmarks show that Flow-CLIP improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment through local evidence refinement, while cross-image ranking supervision mitigates reliance on language priors. Code will be released at link.
evidence_items.title: Flow-CLIP: Image-Conditioned Residual Scoring for CompositionalImage-Text Matching

evidence_items.summary: Cybersecurity interviews uncover critical security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns often not fully captured by conventional technical assessments. Consequently, identifying genuine self-disclosures is challenging because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretations may introduce unsupported claims. Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) protect sensitive participant data by keeping processing within controlled environments, but their limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis. This study developed CARE-SD (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure), a novel four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. We evaluated three local SLMs, including Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, and Llama 3B, using 82 independently annotated cybersecurity interviews across five organizational sectors. Comparisons included conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, larger 8B--32B models, and architectural ablations. Two independent reviewers assessed disclosure labels, factual claims, and explanation correctness. CARE-SD improved the accuracy and evidence reliability of SLMs, increasing Llama 3B Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while reducing unsupported claims by 60\%. Remarkably, the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the architecture without requiring a larger model.
evidence_items.title: CARE-SD: Explainable Reasoning Architecture for Local SLM Self-Disclosure Analysis in Textual Data

evidence_items.summary: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.
evidence_items.title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models

evidence_items.summary: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation--maximization that alternates question-specific context estimation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions under the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging $+9.10$ percentage points. With the same judge, it adds $+1.53$ points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-$N$ are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates. The coverage--selection gap motivates allocating test-time computation jointly to candidate generation and verification.
evidence_items.title: EMO: A Closed-Loop Test-Time Computation Framework via Alternating Context Optimization and Logits Steering

evidence_items.summary: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement. Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.
evidence_items.title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning from internal feedback can improve language models without ground-truth answers or external verifiers. However, confidence and correctness can diverge during training, and continued optimization of average self-certainty can increase confidence while degrading reasoning accuracy. We introduce SIF, a reinforcement learning method that combines comparative reward construction with selective policy updates. SIF compares ranked token-level self-certainty profiles across multiple windows and peers, assigning positive rewards only when both levels of voting provide sufficient support. Sample and group level filtering determines which responses contribute to policy optimization. Experiments on three backbones across 12 mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks show that SIF's final checkpoints achieve higher average accuracy than the best-validation checkpoints of Intuitor and Vigor, with a gain of 4.71 percentage points over Intuitor on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. Further analyses show better retention of accuracy during continued optimization, while test-time training experiments demonstrate sustained improvements with as few as four rollouts per prompt.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Reason with Selective Internal Feedback

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to critically discuss the fast-moving rollout of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and conversational agents as purported remedies to loneliness and social isolation, analysing the fact that the creation of companionship by algorithms substitutes a one-way connection and fundamentally jeopardises real social inclusion.
 
 
 
 An interdisciplinary perspective that draws from relational sociology, the social model of disability, critical digital studies and various literatures on psychiatric rehabilitation to critique the inter-personal ethics, psychological dangers and political economy of digital mental health companions. It also comprises a comparative analysis of the existing market leaders in conversational AI.
 
 
 
 Proximate affective containment is provided by generative AI, but lacks of relational reciprocity, moral agency and shared vulnerability. The replacement of civic infrastructures in community settings by automated, conversational agents can set up a divided mental health system: human-centred relational mental health care for the privileged and synthetic, automated containment for the marginalised service user. Moreover, AI companionship takes out user vulnerability as property information, turns it into a commodity, the lived experience of solitude.
 
 
 
 As a perspective, this paper does not contain empirical data of its own; it constructs the argument by conceptual synthesis instead of a systematic review, and the examples of markets discussed (e.g. Woebot, Wysa, Replika) are illustrative, but not comprehensive or evaluative of current versions of products and so may have changed significantly since the time of writing. Longitudinal studies that compare the outcomes of service users using algorithmic companionship with peer-support and Clubhouse models will confirm the synthetic inclusion construct developed here, and could be used for future research.
 
 
 
 Offers evaluative tools to the mental health commissioners, clinicians and third sector organisations to avoid the “community replacement” trap of digital engagement, keeping AI a cognitive prosthetic and not a substitute for interpersonal interactions.
 
 
 
 Disciplines policymakers from adopting techno-solutionism as an excuse for austerity-driven disinvestment of physical community centres, peer respites and inclusive civic spaces and calls for the protection of the human social commons.
 
 
 
 This paper outlines the concept of a “synthetic inclusion” that reveals that the illusion of connection created by conversational AI is a commodity, and that social isolation is structurally reinforced. It contributes to the critique of mental health in the digital age by examining unconstrained large language models from a perspective of surveillance capitalism and intersectionality.
evidence_items.title: The illusion of algorithmic belonging: why generative AI cannot substitute for relational reciprocity in mental health social inclusion

evidence_items.summary:
This study examines whether the association between audit quality and corporate tax avoidance (TA) is heterogeneous across the TA distribution and whether it differs between listed and non-listed firms. Prior evidence is limited and inconclusive, with sign reversals across settings and specifications. We address this gap by jointly analysing both firm types and applying quantile regression to document distributional variation.
 
 
 
 We apply quantile regression to a sample of Spanish firms (2008–2019), using two audit quality proxies (BIG4 and TENURE), estimating the models separately for listed and non-listed firms and using Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE) estimates as linear benchmarks.
 
 
 
 For non-listed firms, both proxies exhibit heterogeneous associations across the TA distribution. BIG4 is associated with higher tax burdens among conservative firms and with larger book–tax gaps in the upper part of the BTG distribution, while TENURE displays a sign reversal across the BTG distribution. For listed firms, BIG4 shows a broadly homogeneous association with higher tax burdens, whereas TENURE shows no significant association. These patterns are largely obscured under mean-based estimation.
 
 
 
 To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the audit quality–TA association in listed and non-listed firms within the same institutional setting using quantile regression, documenting substantial differences between the two groups. We incorporate auditor tenure alongside BIG4, capturing a less-explored dimension of audit quality, and develop an asymmetric cost–benefit framework suggesting that prior mixed evidence may reflect mean-based estimators rather than underlying contradictions.
evidence_items.title: Tax avoidance and audit quality: evidence from Spanish listed and non-listed companies

evidence_items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is diffusing across higher education, yet institutional governance struggles to adapt in resource-constrained settings. Existing research emphasizes adoption and acceptance, with less attention to how infrastructure and governance shape institutional readiness. This study investigates GenAI governance in Ghanaian higher education. A sequential multi-method design combined the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). DEMATEL drew on a 12-member expert panel to diagnose perceived influence among institutional factors, while PLS-SEM independently evaluated a literature-derived model using 792 student and faculty responses. Resource Sensitivity (RS) emerged as the strongest net-source factor in the expert-perceived influence structure (D−R = +3.685). In the PLS-SEM model, RS was negatively associated with Institutional Readiness (IR) (β = −0.295), whereas Technological Governance Architecture (TGA) was positively associated with IR (β = 0.454); the model explained 48.4% of IR variance (R2 = 0.484). The RS → TGA → IR indirect association was significant (β = −0.061), consistent with complementary partial mediation. AI Literacy (AIL) showed no significant direct association with adoption-related risk, conceptualized as the Adoption–Risk Paradox (ARP), but showed a significant indirect association through Perceived Usefulness (PU). Policy Uncertainty (PUC) was positively associated with ARP, whereas TGA was negatively associated with it. The findings support a Hard–Soft Governance Gap in which infrastructural constraints and governance capability constitute distinct but interconnected conditions of readiness. Strengthening responsible GenAI integration requires coordinated attention to infrastructure, governance, policy clarity, and responsible-use practices.
evidence_items.title: Institutional readiness for generative artificial intelligence is linked to resource constraints and governance capability in Ghanaian higher education

evidence_items.summary: IntroductionReal-time artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support systems are increasingly proposed for use in endoscopic and minimally invasive surgery although how best to present such information intraoperatively is unclear. This study explored surgeon perspectives regarding the user-interface, interpretation and workflow integration of a prototype AI system (CLASSICA-OR) for real-time endoscopic cancer characterization during surgery.MethodsSurgeons specialising in minimally invasive gastrointestinal surgery were asked for their first impressions in their evaluation of the CLASSICA-OR system within a high-fidelity surgical simulation environment. For this, participants viewed prerecorded colonoscopic imagery of significant rectal neoplasia while the AI analysis was applied in real-time to the video. Commentary and responses to semi-structured interview were recorded audiovisually for transcription and analysis using qualitative thematic analysis supported by NVivo (Lumivero).ResultsEighteen surgeons participated, generating rich qualitative data. Four major themes emerged: (1) AI was viewed as a valuable but evolving decision-support tool; (2) institutional culture, governance and commercial realities were recognised as important determinants of adoption; (3) real-time perfusion-based lesion characterisation (foundational to CLASSICA-OR) was considered promising but with specific challenges; and (4) clarity, usability, transparency and workflow compatibility are surgeon priorities in decision-support displays. Participants emphasised minimised cognitive load, preserved surgeon autonomy, clear communication of uncertainty and seamless workflow integration. Preferences differed between simplified binary outputs and more detailed numerical displays supporting the need for adaptable interfaces.ConclusionsSurgeons perceive real-time intraoperative AI decision support as promising but requiring thoughtful user-centred design. They articulate practical development and implementation insights for intraoperative AI systems.
evidence_items.title: Surgeon-Derived Design Insights Regarding Real-Time Artificial Intelligence Decision Support for Endoscopic Cancer Surgery.

evidence_items.summary: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.

evidence_items.summary: In today’s technological age, artificial intelligence literacy (AIL) has become a critical issue in the field of education. The ability to understand, use, and critically evaluate artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is recognized as a fundamental competency enabling students to actively participate in the digital age. In this context, the aim of this study is to develop a valid and reliable scale to obtain accurate data on artificial intelligence literacy by examining the concept of artificial intelligence literacy. The study sample consists of 870 students (424 boys, 346 girls) in grades 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 attending elementary and middle schools. A pool of 50 items was created to measure students’ levels of artificial intelligence literacy. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) resulted in 22 items and 6 subscales. The measurement model obtained from Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) demonstrated good fit. The Cronbach’s Alpha internal consistency coefficient for the scale was found to be 0.857, while the internal consistency coefficients for the subscales ranged between 0.81 and 0.82. The CR, AVE, MSV, and ASV values indicate that the scale possesses both discriminant and convergent validity. In conclusion, the developed scale possesses sufficient characteristics to determine students’ levels of AIL. This study will assist in the development, teaching, and learning of AIL, as well as in the evaluation of AI education.
evidence_items.title: Development and validation of an artificial intelligence literacy scale for students

evidence_items.summary:
This study aims to investigate the effect of utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in social commerce on increasing consumer engagement, specifically in terms of engagement and conversion rates. It also examines the role of flow experience in strengthening this relationship.
 
 
 
 This study collected data from 354 Indonesian social commerce shoppers. Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling was employed to analyze the data following the two-stage procedure. First, the measurement model was assessed for validity and reliability. Second, the structural hypothesis model was evaluated to test the proposed hypotheses.
 
 
 
 The utilization of AI significantly influences social commerce visitor interactions in terms of engagement and conversion. Both variables can enhance customer satisfaction, thereby impacting repurchase intention. Flow experience also strengthens the relationship between engagement and satisfaction, offering practical guidance for creating immersive and enjoyable user experiences.
 
 
 
 This study extends the existing social commerce and AI literature by positioning flow experience as a moderator, explaining how and when engagement and conversion translate into satisfaction. Unlike previous models that primarily focus on direct effects, this research introduces psychological mechanisms that capture the conditional and experiential nature of AI-driven interactions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of consumer behavior in social commerce.
evidence_items.title: Exploring the moderating effects of flow experience in strengthening artificial intelligence-based customer interactions on social commerce

evidence_items.summary: The brain and eye share profound and homologous relationships in terms of development, anatomy, and microcirculatory structures, yet current analyses typically examine them in isolation, limiting cross-organ insights and the development of integrated artificial intelligence (AI) models. Such a fragmented paradigm also constrains clinical understanding despite growing evidence of shared, anatomically connected, and predictive relationships between ocular and cerebral phenotypes in both brain and eye diseases. In this context, this review introduces an Eye-Brain Connection Pyramid, a multiscale organizational framework for examining eye-brain relationships at three complementary biological levels: genetic and genomic susceptibility, molecular and protein processes, and neurovascular and tissue phenotypes. The pyramid does not represent a serial causal pathway. Across these levels, the framework distinguishes shared vulnerability and parallel pathology, direct brain-to-eye effects, retinal correlates and predictors of cerebral or systemic disease, and putative eye-to-brain causal contributions, which remain insufficiently established in humans. This framework may inform future clinical research and the development of AI models integrating multimodal cross-organ data, whose incremental diagnostic value over existing single-organ and clinical approaches requires prospective validation. Furthermore, this review presents a comprehensive AI research roadmap, spanning longitudinal prognostic models, explainable algorithms for clinical adoption, validation of incremental clinical value, fundus-based brain health screening setups, and multi-site collaboration. By outlining these priorities, the proposed Eye-Brain Connection Pyramid provides an organizational framework for investigating integrated eye-brain diagnostics and for evaluating the potential clinical value of cross-organ AI in risk stratification, longitudinal monitoring, and healthcare delivery.
evidence_items.title: Towards Next-Generation Artificial Intelligence Models for Integrated Diagnostics Embedding Eye-Brain Connections

evidence_items.summary: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology. Methods A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility. Results Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models. Conclusions The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and trustworthy while maximizing their potential to improve patient care.
evidence_items.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) data represents a burgeoning frontier in schizophrenia diagnostics. However, the inferential validity of findings is frequently compromised by methodological heterogeneity. This systematic review rigorously evaluates the diagnostic efficacy and methodological robustness of AI-generated EEG biomarkers by implementing the Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool for Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST+AI). Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 43 primary studies encompassing 3,420 patients with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis and 3,164 healthy controls (total N = 6,584). Methodological quality and validation strategies were assessed using the 34 signaling questions of the PROBAST+AI framework. Results The aggregate mean diagnostic accuracy across the literature was 93.38%, with deep learning architectures demonstrating superior metrics relative to classical machine learning (96.83% vs. 87.68%). Critically, external validation was restricted to 4.7% of the included studies. A pronounced performance discrepancy was observed between subject-wise (88.22%) and segment-wise (98.14%) validation protocols, indicating pervasive data leakage. Overall, 76.7% of the analyzed studies were characterized by a high risk of bias, predominantly stemming from suboptimal data partitioning and inadequate independent verification. Conclusions Contemporary diagnostic accuracies appear to be artifactually elevated due to structural methodological deficiencies and data leakage. Consequently, current evidence does not support the immediate clinical implementation of AI-EEG biomarkers in schizophrenia. To facilitate translational progress, we propose a standardized methodological framework optimizing validation strategies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence EEG biomarkers for schizophrenia diagnosis: Systematic review with PROBAST+AI assessment

evidence_items.summary: This evidence-based critical review examines how emerging artificial-intelligence (AI) capabilities can strengthen resilient smart-grid fault intelligence. Rather than comparing algorithms primarily by reported accuracy, the review organizes recent fault-detection evidence around operational capabilities: spatial/topology awareness, temporal context, label efficiency, physical consistency, trust and uncertainty, privacy-preserving collaboration, and deployment feasibility. A structured primary-study evidence matrix was developed to extract task, system or dataset, topology, temporal context, robustness, trust, privacy, physics, deployment evidence, and principal limitations. The extracted evidence shows a clear asymmetry in the maturity of emerging approaches. Recent Transformer work demonstrates real-time temporal fault detection on test-system waveforms, self-supervised methods reduce dependence on manually labeled events, physics-informed approaches can narrow the simulation-to-field gap, and graph-based models increasingly address topology and cross-topology generalization. However, external validation, uncertainty quantification, reproducibility, and standardized deployment evidence remain uneven. Based on this evidence, the paper introduces a fault-intelligence evidence maturity profile that avoids reducing readiness to a single generic score. The synthesis leads to an evidence-derived roadmap progressing from trustworthy and data-efficient intelligence to topology- and physics-aware learning, distributed cyber-physical intelligence, and finally integrated safety-bounded decision support. The review deliberately distinguishes demonstrated evidence from plausible future capability and therefore avoids unsupported claims of algorithmic superiority.
evidence_items.title: Emerging AI for resilient smart-grid fault detection: an evidence-based capability synthesis, maturity assessment, and research roadmap

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation.


METHODS
This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions.


RESULTS
Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77).


CONCLUSIONS
AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.
evidence_items.title: Impact of AI-Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real-World Study.

evidence_items.summary: The convergence of blockchain, financial technology, digital assets, and generative artificial intelligence creates important opportunities and challenges for undergraduate education, especially at Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Students preparing for careers in business, computing, analytics, cybersecurity, and financial services need more than exposure to emerging technologies; they also need confidence, collaboration skills, ethical awareness, computational fluency, and experience applying tools to realistic problems. This paper proposes a human-centered pedagogical framework to engage HBCU students in active learning about blockchain, FinTech, and generative AI. The framework synthesizes classroom-tested strategies from computer information systems, business analytics, programming, mathematics, and interdisciplinary student research. It emphasizes structured collaboration, low-stakes practice, role rotation, peer evaluation, reflective learning, responsible use of generative AI, reproducible computational notebooks, and applied problem contexts such as credit risk, fraud detection, investment analysis, digital trust, and smart financial systems. The paper presents an evidence-informed model that instructors can adapt across introductory and advanced undergraduate courses. The framework suggests that active, collaborative, and AI-supported pedagogy can increase student participation, reduce anxiety around technical topics, support inclusive learning, and strengthen workforce readiness for emerging blockchain and FinTech ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Engaging HBCU Students in Active Learning for Blockchain, FinTech, and Generative AI: A Human-Centered Pedagogical Framework

evidence_items.summary: The rapid expansion of blockchain technology and digital asset markets has increased the demand for intelligent tools capable of evaluating cryptocurrency performance using real-time financial data. As cryptocurrency markets become more dynamic and interconnected, investors, researchers, and financial technology practitioners require timely, data-driven insights to support informed investment decisions (Lazea et al., 2026). While numerous market platforms provide real-time price information, relatively few integrate live market data, technical analysis, artificial intelligence (AI), and comparative analytics within a unified decision-support environment. The study demonstrates how integrating live market data, technical analysis, and AI-driven analytics within a browser-based platform enables transparent and efficient comparative evaluation of leading cryptocurrency assets. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for assessing digital asset performance and supports investment decision-making while offering a scalable foundation for future research involving alternative cryptocurrencies, sector-specific digital assets, and extended market periods.
evidence_items.title: AI-Powered Comparative Analysis of the Top Five Cryptocurrency Assets Using Real-Time Market Data

evidence_items.summary: Cultural industries have emerged as an increasingly important component of contemporary economic development, by bringing together cultural expression, creativity, technology, intellectual property, and market mechanisms. Unlike traditional industries, cultural industries generate economic value not only through material production but also through symbolic meanings, cultural identities, knowledge, and creative content. The expansion of digital technologies, streaming platforms, social media, artificial intelligence, and global cultural markets has further transformed the production, distribution, and consumption of cultural products. These developments have created additional opportunities for developing countries to participate in global value chains while simultaneously creating challenges related to cultural identity, intellectual property protection, market concentration, inequality, and the commercialization of culture. Vietnam represents an important case in this transformation because the country possesses considerable cultural diversity, traditional craft heritage, performing arts, historical resources, and a rapidly expanding digital economy. Since the adoption of the National Strategy for the Development of Cultural Industries to 2020, with a Vision to 2030, Vietnam has increasingly recognized cultural industries as an economic sector capable of contributing to employment, economic growth, tourism, national branding, and international integration. This article examines the theoretical foundations of cultural industries, analyzes their economic and social significance, evaluates the development of cultural industries in Vietnam, and discusses the opportunities and challenges created by digitalization and globalization. The article argues that Vietnam should move beyond viewing culture primarily as a field of preservation or public expenditure and increasingly recognize culture as a productive resource while maintaining cultural diversity, public value, and social inclusion. The future development of Vietnamese cultural industries therefore requires an integrated ecosystem connecting creativity, education, technology, intellectual property protection, finance, entrepreneurship, cultural heritage, and international markets.
evidence_items.title: Cultural Industries and Their Development in Vietnam: Economic Transformation, Cultural Value, and Creative Potential

evidence_items.summary:
This practitioner case study addresses the persistent gap between smart city aspirations and implementable urban operator practice by examining how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled methods can be operationalised across the full infrastructure lifecycle within real infrastructure operator workflows.
 
 
 
 The framework integrates four AI-enabled operational tools – GeoAI satellite asset mapping, a fuzzy-logic engine encoding national lighting standards, a Bayesian predictive maintenance model designed for data-scarce contexts and an adaptive lighting control system. The artefacts were deployed and evaluated through naturalistic pilots and retrospective analyses in municipalities in Italy, Spain and Chile.
 
 
 
 Deployment evidence (operationally observed, not from controlled experiments) shows 82–92% asset detection accuracy across sites, ∼70% design effort reduction, ∼20% maintenance efficiency gain and ∼35% energy savings beyond light-emitting diode baselines. Cross-site deployment yielded five transferable design principles for scalable, regulation-aware governance of AI-enabled civic infrastructure.
 
 
 
 The framework provides actionable guidance for municipal administrators and infrastructure operators pursuing AI-enabled infrastructure governance, contributing to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities).
 
 
 
 This study contributes an operationally validated governance framework that moves beyond isolated smart city pilots by embedding heterogeneous AI tools into systemic lifecycle management under real-world institutional and regulatory constraints.
evidence_items.title: Data-driven lifecycle governance for intelligent public lighting: a multi-city deployment study

evidence_items.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.
evidence_items.title: The Dormant Spiking Neuron: A State-Driven Mechanism for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks

evidence_items.summary:
This paper proposes a pedagogical framework for cultivating inquiry-driven agency in student engagement with artificial intelligence (AI). It addresses a gap in the AI-in-education literature, in which substantial scholarly attention to material access and algorithmic fairness has been accompanied by comparatively less sustained attention to the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. The paper offers three connected contributions: a cyclical model of inquiry-driven learning, a four-phase curricular sequence for student-AI engagement, and an operational assessment counterpart that remains diagnostically meaningful in AI-mediated environments.
 
 
 
 The paper employs an integrative conceptual approach in the tradition of model-paper scholarship (Jaakkola, 2020). It synthesises five bodies of literature: AI in education and AI literacy frameworks, critical scholarship on educational technology, foundational work on curiosity, dual-process cognition, and adaptive expertise, constructive-developmental theory, and research on question-asking in learning and authentic assessment. Sources were identified through targeted citation tracing supplemented by database searches. Theoretical resources are justified at the point of use rather than methodologically up front.
 
 
 
 The analysis demonstrates that material access and algorithmic fairness, while necessary, do not on their own account for the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. It argues that inquiry-driven agency, the capacity to ask productive questions of AI rather than receive its answers, is a worthwhile object of pedagogical design. The Student-AI Learning Trajectory Model presents this development as a four-phase curricular sequence (AI as Tool, Machine, Object, and Partner), with progression understood as a curricular design decision made by educators rather than a developmental trigger inside the learner.
 
 
 
 The model is conceptual rather than empirically validated, and its applicability to younger learners, neurodiverse learners, and low-literacy contexts has not been fully worked out. The paper signposts several lines of empirical inquiry: longitudinal studies of SALT-informed curricula, methodological development of inquiry-sequence assessment instruments drawing on the Objective Structured Clinical Examination tradition, and comparative studies across institutional contexts and learner populations. The contribution is bounded to the pedagogical dimension and does not address the structural reforms that critical scholarship has identified as necessary for genuine educational equity.
 
 
 
 The paper has implications for curriculum design, educator development, and assessment practice. Curricula can sequence student-AI engagement across phases of increasing sophistication rather than treating AI literacy as content to be covered. Educator development requires sustained investment in pedagogical capacity, particularly the modelling of inquiry-driven engagement in front of students. Institutions should treat the redesign of assessment for the AI era as a pedagogical question rather than an integrity question, with inquiry-sequence assessment offering one operational direction. Equity-oriented investment should prioritise educator capacity over the mass distribution of adaptive learning software.
 
 
 
 The cultivation of inquiry capacity in AI-mediated learning environments matters for the kinds of learners that schools and universities send into a world increasingly shaped by automated systems. Without deliberate pedagogical design, AI risks becoming a multiplier of existing educational divides rather than a neutralising force. The model locates responsibility with institutions and educators designing learning environments, not with individual students, and identifies the risk of a pedagogical Matthew Effect in which inquiry-driven pedagogy becomes available primarily to already advantaged students absent institutional investment in educator capacity.
 
 
 
 The paper brings together three conversations that have developed largely in parallel: AI literacy as a set of competencies, evaluative judgement as a response to generative AI's destabilisation of assessment, and curiosity as a driver of self-directed learning. Its distinctive contribution is the articulation of phase progression as a curricular sequence informed by a cyclical model of inquiry learning, complemented by an operational assessment counterpart. The paper offers vocabulary and tools for educators, curriculum designers, and assessment scholars responding to the question of how AI should be integrated into the work of cultivating independent learners.
evidence_items.title: Beyond access and algorithms: a curricular model for inquiry-driven student-AI engagement

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven lifestyle interventions are increasingly used for reducing diabetes risk. However, whether they produce clinical benefit beyond standard Diabetes Prevention Programs (DPPs) and whether effects vary by AI type, population, or delivery setting, remains uncertain.


OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to evaluate the effects of AI-driven lifestyle interventions on clinical, behavioral, and engagement outcomes among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risk and to assess whether effects differed by AI type, population, or delivery setting.


METHODS
PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ClinicalTrials.gov, and citation searches were completed on August 3, 2026, for English-language reports published from 2015. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven digital lifestyle interventions among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risks, or healthy participants in feasibility studies. One reviewer (OIE) screened records and extracted data; a second reviewer (TN) independently verified exclusions and extraction. Study quality was assessed with National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tools appropriate to each design. Given substantial heterogeneity in designs, estimands, and outcome metrics, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline rather than pooled statistically.


RESULTS
Of 8032 records, 11 studies were included: 1 randomized, 1 nonrandomized comparative, 4 observational, and 5 uncontrolled pre-post studies. Seven evaluated AI lifestyle coaching systems, 2 predictive AI platforms, and 2 conversational AI chatbots. Ten of 11 studies used commercially developed platforms. Study quality was rated good for 5 studies, fair for 3, and poor for 3. The randomized controlled trial showed noninferiority of an AI-DPP versus human coach-led DPP for the combined 12-month outcome (23/183, 12.6% vs 23/185, 12.4%; risk difference 0.1%, 1-sided 95% CI -5.5%). Program initiation (171/183, 93.4% vs 153/185, 82.7%; risk difference 10.7%, 95% CI 4.2%-17.3%) and completion (117/183, 63.9% vs 93/185, 50.3%; risk difference 13.7%; 95% CI 3.6%-23.7%) were higher with AI, but this did not translate into superior clinical outcomes. The nonrandomized comparison found no advantage of AI-personalized messaging over static messaging in terms of BMI or physical activity. The remaining studies reported uncontrolled changes precluding causal inference. Evidence was insufficient to determine whether effects differed by population or delivery setting.


CONCLUSIONS
One randomized trial supports noninferiority, not superiority, of a specific AI-driven DPP relative to human coaching; the remaining evidence was nonrandomized, predominantly commercially developed, and hypothesis-generating. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to stratify evidence on AI-driven diabetes prevention by AI mechanism-coaching, predictive, and conversational-and by outcome domain, extending prior scoping work that mapped apps without appraising study quality or comparative effectiveness. This structured mapping shows where evidence is the strongest (engagement and weight) and the weakest (glycemic causality and generalizability), giving health systems a concrete basis for deciding where AI-DPP tools may supplement, rather than replace, standard DPP delivery, pending independent, adequately powered randomized trials.
evidence_items.title: AI-Driven Lifestyle Interventions for Reducing Diabetes Risk: Systematic Review.

evidence_items.summary: With the advent of Covid-19, it is necessary to repurpose new treatment alternatives, either in the form of an effective single dose of these antidiabetic drug agents or an efficacious combination of them for elderly population with or had suffered this condition. Newer medication classes for diabetes have been increasing in use, and their utilization varied across provinces and how the COVID-19 pandemic may have affected these trends. This mini review has the objective of predicting the targets of bioactive small molecules in human using healthcare applied artificial intelligence. These substances in the body are target specific receptors on the surface of cells, and antidiabetic drugs contains moiety´s and functional groups that may act on one or several subtypes of receptors. The tool is a tuned algorithm, with novel data bank in web interface. Information figures of Swiss Target Prediction (STP), which allow predictions on therapy combinations and probable side effects, were reordered. The bibliographic databases were searched to identify existing cost studies, economic evaluations and models, and most of the parameters were derived from the published literatura. Predictions are done using a ligand-based approach, based on the similarity between a query molecule and the known ligands of a large collection of protein targets. The result of this study highlighted crucial recommendations for the use of some of the antidiabetic agent groups in diabetic patients. Our findings provide real world evidence supporting the potential clinical benefits of diabetes drug agents in mitigating side effects and development in patients with T2DM.
evidence_items.title: Antidiabetic drugs and its pharmacological profile target in human for type 2 diabetes mellitus

evidence_items.summary: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.
evidence_items.title: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Atrial cardiomyopathy (AtCM) is increasingly recognised as an underlying atrial substrate contributing to atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and cardio-embolic stroke. However, diagnostic criteria, disease thresholds, and targeted treatment strategies remain poorly defined.


OBJECTIVE
To describe the rationale, structure, and translational strategy of the EmbRACE (Electro-Molecular Basis and the theRapeutic management of Atrial Cardiomyopathy, fibrillation and associated outcomEs) network, a national consortium established to address key knowledge gaps in AtCM.


METHODS
EmbRACE integrates mechanistic research, computational modelling, clinical trials, and implementation science within seven interconnected work packages. Human atrial tissue biobanking and deep phenotyping (WP1) enable molecular profiling of candidate pathways (WP2), which are validated in experimental models (WP3). Computational modelling and artificial intelligence (WP4) integrate multimodal clinical and biological data to derive composite AtCM phenotypes and severity frameworks. Substrate-targeting clinical trials evaluate AF ablation (RACE X; WP5), weight reduction using GLP‑1 agonists (DUTCH-WAIST; WP6), and optimised rate control using calcium channel antagonists (SMART-VERAPAF; WP6). Implementation science (WP7) focuses on guideline integration, decision-support tools, and governance of AI-based risk models. EmbRACE establishes a translational pipeline from mechanistic discovery to clinical application. By integrating tissue-level insights with multimodal risk modelling and interventional trials, the consortium aims to define clinically meaningful AtCM thresholds, to validate indirect markers, and to determine whether targeted treatment modifies disease progression and clinical outcomes.


CONCLUSION
EmbRACE provides a multidisciplinary framework to transform AtCM from a theoretical construct into a clinically actionable entity, enabling earlier detection, improved risk stratification, and AtCM-directed therapy in cardiovascular prevention.
evidence_items.title: Atrial cardiomyopathy: from knowledge gaps to clinical impact : The role of the EmbRACE Network.

evidence_items.summary: Multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) control depends on identifying colonized patients and emerging transmission events early enough to intervene, without overwhelming infection prevention and control (IPC) teams or unnecessarily isolating patients. Predictive models using electronic health records, microbiology data, patient movement, and genomic information may support this task. We propose a practical Predict → Confirm → Act framework for artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented infection control across hospitals and long-term care facilities. In this framework, AI generates risk signals; microbiology, genomic data, and epidemiological review provide confirmation; and IPC teams apply proportionate actions such as targeted screening, preemptive precautions, cohorting, environmental investigation, or de-escalation. The framework is model-agnostic and is intended to shift attention away from algorithmic performance alone toward bedside and unit-level decisions. Safe implementation requires local threshold calibration, named alert ownership, microbiological confirmation pathways, de-escalation rules, prospective monitoring, and evaluation using IPC-relevant outcomes, including additional carriers detected, time to isolation, MDRO acquisition, isolation days avoided, alert burden, and unintended consequences.
evidence_items.title: A Predict → Confirm → Act Framework for AI-Augmented MDRO Control Across Hospitals and Long-Term Care Facilities.

evidence_items.summary:
This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment, focusing on the underexplored role of AI virtual assistants (AIVA). This study aims to evaluate how AIVA transforms recruitment practices and to provide a systematic research agenda for future applications.
 
 
 
 The authors conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) and a bibliometric analysis (BA) to assess the use of AIVA in recruitment over the past decade, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. A structured search of the Scopus and Web of Science databases identified 5,301 publications from 2015 to June 1, 2026. After screening, the authors selected 255 papers for full-text review and BA, using R and VOSviewer. They systematically summarized and guided the exploration of current research.
 
 
 
 The findings suggest that AIVA affects every phase of the recruitment process, from identifying staffing requirements to onboarding new personnel, with publications increasing significantly after 2023. The thematic analysis identified four key themes: isolated mature areas, innovation drivers, transitional uncertainties and broad foundational concepts. In addition, this SLR and BA critically examined the existing literature, highlighting advances and identifying gaps for future research. It also proposed a research agenda to guide subsequent investigations.
 
 
 
 This study is limited to publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, which potentially excludes relevant literature. Future research should expand to diverse data sets and explore the longitudinal impacts of AIVA adoption.
 
 
 
 The findings provide actionable pathways for Human Resources (HR) practitioners to integrate AIVA into recruitment, thereby improving decision-making and reducing inefficiencies.
 
 
 
 AIVA adoption may improve recruitment equity, fairness, inclusivity and efficiency.
 
 
 
 This paper uniquely synthesizes recruitment literature on AIVA through a dual SLR and BA approach. It advances theory by operationalizing broad AI research directions into domain-specific insights and offers practical implications for reducing recruitment costs, enhancing efficiency and guiding stakeholders in adopting AIVA.
evidence_items.title: AI virtual assistance in recruitment: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI-generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi-frame visual evidence, and prompt-independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment-level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123-123/VGCap.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Source Prompts: Towards Visually Grounded AI-Generated Video Quality Assessment

evidence_items.summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools.
 
 
 
 The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable.
 
 
 
 Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains.
 
 
 
 The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity.
 
 
 
 The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. Given that daily users show higher critical evaluation but lower perceived accuracy, teaching practices should incorporate reflective assignments that require students to justify, critique and revise AI-generated content. Assessment formats may need redesign to ensure transparent AI use while still requiring independent reasoning, analytical justification and domain-specific understanding.
 
 
 
 Policies should balance the productivity benefits of AI-supported learning with safeguards that promote independent thinking, academic integrity and equitable access. Addressing disparities in AI literacy and access is essential to prevent the widening of the existing academic inequalities.
 
 
 
 This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-assisted learning by examining students’ perceived productivity gains alongside several concurrent dimensions of their AI-supported academic experience, including time efficiency, perceived academic performance, academic self-efficacy, changes in cognitive effort and AI dependency. Rather than proposing these dimensions as new constructs or causal mechanisms, this study brings them together within a single analytical framework. Particular attention is given to whether perceived productivity gains and growing reliance on AI coexist with self-reported changes in cognitive effort, an interplay that remains insufficiently explored in the existing research. Empirically, this study provides exploratory evidence from Vietnam, an underrepresented higher education context in Southeast Asia.
evidence_items.title: AI in education: boosting productivity or challenging cognitive effort?

evidence_items.summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial technology (FinTech) has transformed the delivery of banking, lending, and financial management services across the global economy. For underserved communities, including low-income and historically marginalized populations, AI-powered financial systems present both significant opportunities and emerging risks. This paper examines how AI-driven FinTech applications can expand financial inclusion by increasing access to digital banking, personalized financial education, automated credit assessment, fraud detection, and alternative lending solutions. The study also explores how data analytics and machine learning models are reshaping financial decision- making processes within decentralized and technology-driven financial ecosystems. Despite these advancements, concerns remain regarding algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital literacy gaps, and unequal access to technological infrastructure. AI systems trained on historically biased financial data may unintentionally reinforce discriminatory lending patterns and economic disparities, particularly among underserved populations. Additionally, the increasing dependence on automated financial systems raises questions surrounding transparency, accountability, and regulatory oversight within emerging financial technologies. Using a qualitative analysis of existing literature, industry reports, and current FinTech case studies, this paper evaluates both the benefits and challenges of AI adoption in financial services. The findings suggest that while AI has the potential to promote greater economic participation and financial accessibility, ethical implementation, deterministic AI frameworks, and inclusive regulatory policies are necessary to ensure equitable outcomes. This research contributes to ongoing discussions regarding the societal implications of AI-driven financial innovation and the future of inclusive digital finance.
evidence_items.title: Financial Inclusion in the Age of AI: Opportunities and Risks for Underserved Communities

evidence_items.summary: The rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) following the public release of tools such as ChatGPT has begun to reshape how students engage with coding, statistical analysis, and written communication in higher education. Growing use of conversational AI systems creates opportunities for learning alongside challenges around reliability, transparency, privacy, and appropriate academic and professional practice, highlighting the need for structured education in their responsible use. This paper presents a framework for teaching the responsible and effective use of generative AI in statistics and data science. The framework is organised around four areas: Understanding, Development, Reporting, and Safety, covering conceptual foundations, practical interaction within analytical workflows, documentation and transparency, and issues including reliability, bias, privacy, and ethics. Its design draws on emerging work in AI literacy and established principles from statistics and data science education, and was further refined through workshop and conference activities and participant feedback. The framework has been implemented across multiple settings, including a massive open online course, short training sessions, and undergraduate and postgraduate skills-based teaching.
